title: Separating mixtures: every method uses one difference between the parts

summary.text: Stir one mustard seed into a katori of rava and you can pick the seed out again. Stir in a pinch of salt and you cannot, though the salt is still there. Why does one come back so easily and the other not? In this lesson you separate mixtures by picking, sieving, a magnet, filtering and evaporation, and you find that each method works by using one difference between the parts. Then you ask a harder question: clear water looks like one material, so how would you know if it is?
summary.art: A steel katori of rava with one black mustard seed lifted out and a few white salt grains still hidden in the rava.

intro.hook: Put two spoons of rava in a katori. Drop in one mustard seed and stir. Can you get the seed back? Now stir in a pinch of salt. Can you get the salt back?
intro.text: The mustard seed is black and round, so your eyes find the seed and your fingers lift the seed out. The salt grains are white and small, like the rava, so your eyes and fingers cannot tell them apart. Yet the salt has not turned into rava. Touch a little of the mixture to your tongue and you taste it. So the salt is still salt, and there must be some way to make it leave. Today you will find the ways people, other animals and the Earth use to take a mixture apart. Each time, ask one thing: what is different about the part that leaves?
intro.art: A steel katori of pale rava seen from above, with one black mustard seed easy to spot and a few salt grains that look just like the rava.

outcomes: I can say what a mixture is, and name mixtures that look like one material, such as air, sea water and 22-carat gold.
I can show that a material keeps its own properties inside a mixture, and say which properties of the whole mixture can be new.
I can separate a mixture by picking, sieving, a magnet, settling, filtering and evaporation, and say which difference between the parts each method uses.
I can choose the methods for a mixture of three or four materials, put them in a sensible order, and give my reason for each step.
I can tell how living beings and the Earth separate mixtures, with examples such as a kidney, a flamingo's beak and rain.
I can explain why 'pure' depends on how closely a thing is tested, and name one question about mixing that nobody can answer yet.

explanations.concept: A mixture is two or more materials together, and each one is still itself
explanations.definition: A mixture is two or more materials put together, in which each material stays the same material and can be taken out again without changing it into something else.
explanations.description: Tip a cup of rice into a cup of toor dal and stir. You now have a mixture. Every grain of rice is still rice, and every grain of dal is still dal. Nothing new was made. You could sit and pick the two apart, and you would have the same cup of rice and the same cup of dal. The parts of a mixture can be in any amounts. One spoon of dal in a sack of rice is a mixture, and so is half and half. The parts can be solids, liquids or gases. Salt water is a solid mixed into a liquid. Air is several gases mixed together.
examples: Sambar powder is a mixture of ground chilli, coriander seed, dal, fenugreek and other spices. Each family chooses different amounts.
Soil is a mixture of sand, clay, bits of dead leaves, water, air and many small living beings.
A glass of nimbu pani is a mixture of water, lemon juice, sugar and salt.
The air in your room is a mixture of gases, with dust and water vapour mixed in.

perspectives.who: Cooks and shopkeepers in India
perspectives.explanation: In a kitchen, a mixture is anything made by putting things together, and the amounts are the cook's choice. A masala, a chivda and a fruit salad are all mixtures in this sense. This everyday meaning matches the science meaning well.

perspectives.who: Chemists, since Joseph Proust's work on fixed proportions in about 1799
perspectives.explanation: Chemists add one test. In a mixture the amounts can be anything. In a compound, which is a new material made when materials join, the amounts are always fixed. Water is always two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen. So a chemist asks 'can the amounts vary?' to decide if something is a mixture.

explanations.art: Two cups, one of rice and one of toor dal, with arrows to a third bowl where the grains are mixed, and a zoom circle showing each grain unchanged.
explanations.context: This card says what a mixture is, which is the word the whole lesson stands on.

explanations.concept: A material keeps its own properties inside a mixture
explanations.definition: A property is something a material does or has, such as its colour, its taste, or being attracted by a magnet. In a mixture, each material generally keeps the properties it had before.
explanations.description: Mix iron pins into a bowl of sand. Hold a magnet over the bowl, and the pins jump to it just as they did before. Being mixed with sand did not change the iron. Stir salt into water until you cannot see it. The water tastes salty, because the salt is still salt. This is why separating is possible at all. A method can only pull a material out if that material still behaves in its own way. Scientists say 'generally' because the whole mixture can show something new. Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water does. Neither the salt nor the water does that alone.
examples: A raisin in a bowl of poha is still sweet and still soft.
Sugar stirred into tea has lost its white colour and its crunch, but it has kept its sweetness.
Brass is copper and zinc melted together. Brass is harder than either metal, and that hardness belongs to the mixture.
Dry salt and plain water each carry electricity very poorly. Salt water carries it well.

perspectives.who: School science books, including the Cambridge primary course
perspectives.explanation: They state the rule simply: materials generally keep their properties in a mixture. The rule is right for the properties we use to separate things, such as size, magnetism and dissolving.

perspectives.who: Materials scientists who make alloys
perspectives.explanation: An alloy is a metal mixed with other materials. People who make alloys mix on purpose to get a property that no part has alone. Steel, which is iron with a little carbon, is far stronger than iron. For them the interesting part of a mixture is what is new.

perspectives.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, as reported in Madhava's Sarvadarshanasamgraha, chapter 1, of the 14th century CE
perspectives.explanation: They pointed to fermenting. The ingredients of a fermented drink do not make anyone drunk, but the mixture, after it ferments, does. They used this to argue that a new power can appear when things are combined. Today we know that yeast, who are living beings, change the sugar into a new material, so this is more than a mixture.

explanations.art: A magnet lifting iron pins out of a bowl of sand, beside a tumbler of clear salt water with a child's tongue tasting a drop from a spoon.
explanations.context: This card shows why a mixture can be taken apart: each part still behaves as itself.

explanations.concept: Mixing that makes a new material is not a mixture any more
explanations.definition: When materials join and change into a new material, a chemical change has happened. The new material cannot be taken apart by picking, sieving, a magnet, filtering or evaporation.
explanations.description: Squeeze lemon juice into warm milk. The milk breaks into white lumps and a thin yellow-green liquid. You cannot get smooth milk back. Something new was made. Compare that with salt in water. Leave salt water in a plate in the sun, and the same salt comes back. So here is a test you can use. Ask: 'Can I get the same things back?' If yes, it was a mixture. If the things have changed into something else, a chemical change happened. Many things in the kitchen are both. Dosa batter starts as a mixture of ground rice, urad dal and water. Overnight, bacteria and yeasts living in the batter change part of it, and the sour taste is new.
examples: Wet sand dries back into sand. That was a mixture.
Cement and water set into a hard solid that never becomes powder and water again. That was a chemical change.
A rusty nail is iron that has joined with oxygen. A magnet test and a file will not bring the shiny iron back.

perspectives.who: Chemists
perspectives.explanation: They separate two kinds of change. A physical change, such as mixing, dissolving or melting, leaves each material the same material. A chemical change makes new materials. The methods in this lesson undo only the first kind.

perspectives.who: Chemists who study dissolving closely
perspectives.explanation: They point out that the line is not perfectly sharp. When salt dissolves, each grain comes apart into two kinds of charged particles, called ions, and water molecules gather round each one. Some call that a small chemical change. It still counts as a mixture in school science, because drying brings the same salt back.

explanations.art: Two plates side by side: salt water drying to white salt crystals with a tick, and curdled milk with lumps and a cross showing it cannot go back.
explanations.context: This card marks the edge of the lesson: the methods here work on mixtures, and not on materials that have changed into new ones.

explanations.concept: Every way of separating uses one difference between the parts
explanations.definition: To separate a mixture, find a property in which the parts differ. Then use something that treats the parts differently because of that property.
explanations.description: A sieve does not know what rice is. It only lets small things through and stops big things. A magnet only attracts some metals. Water only dissolves some solids. Each of these treats the parts of a mixture differently for one reason. So before you choose a method, you ask what is different about the parts. Is one bigger? Is one attracted by a magnet? Does one dissolve in water? Does one sink faster? If the parts differ in size, sieve them. If they differ in dissolving, add water. If you can find no difference at all, no method will work. Then you need a closer look, or a new instrument, to find a difference.
examples: Rajma and rava differ in size, so a sieve separates them.
Iron pins and brass pins look alike and are the same size. They differ in being attracted by a magnet.
Salt and fine sand differ in dissolving. Salt dissolves in water and sand does not.
Husk and grain differ in how easily moving air carries them.
explanations.one_view: This is a description of how every separating method works, and no tradition or scientist proposes a method that separates parts with no difference between them.
explanations.art: A chart with four rows, each showing a mixture, the difference between its parts in one word (size, magnet, dissolving, wind) and a small picture of the method.
explanations.context: This card gives the one idea behind all the methods that follow, so that each method is easy to understand and to choose.

explanations.concept: Picking by hand uses a difference the eyes or fingers can tell
explanations.definition: Picking, also called hand-picking, is taking one part out of a mixture one piece at a time, using a difference in colour, shape or size that you can see or feel.
explanations.description: Spread a handful of rice on a steel plate. A small grey stone shows up against the white grains, and you flick it out. That is picking. It needs no tool, only a difference your senses can catch. Picking works well when the unwanted pieces are few and easy to see. It is slow when there are many, and it fails when the pieces are too small or look alike. Picking is still one of the most used methods in the world. Much of India's tea is plucked by hand, two leaves and a bud at a time, mostly by women, because fingers can choose the young leaves from the old.
examples: Taking small stones and bits of husk out of rice or dal before cooking.
Sorting a mixed bag of buttons by colour.
Taking the whole red chillies and curry leaves out of your sambar before you eat.
A sparrow at a heap of swept-up grain and grit picks up the grain and leaves the grit.

perspectives.who: Waste pickers in Indian cities
perspectives.explanation: By different estimates, between 15 lakh and 40 lakh people in India earn their living by picking paper, plastic, glass and metal out of mixed rubbish. They recover a large share of what the country recycles. Their groups, such as the women's cooperative SWaCH in Pune, ask families to keep wet and dry waste apart, because picking through mixed waste is slow and unsafe.

perspectives.who: Engineers who build sorting machines for rice mills
perspectives.explanation: A modern rice mill picks too, with a machine. Grains fall past cameras, and a puff of air knocks out each dark or broken grain. The machine uses the same difference as the eye, which is colour, and checks thousands of grains each second.

explanations.art: A steel plate of rice with a child's finger flicking out a small grey stone, and a few picked stones in a row at the rim.
explanations.context: This card explains the oldest and simplest method, and when it stops working.

explanations.concept: Sieving uses a difference in size
explanations.definition: A sieve is a sheet or net with holes all of one size. Sieving separates pieces smaller than the holes, which fall through, from pieces bigger than the holes, which stay on top.
explanations.description: Shake atta in a sieve. The fine flour falls through, and the brown flakes of bran stay on the mesh. The holes of an atta sieve are less than 1 millimetre across. A piece gets through only if it is smaller than the hole. So the size of the holes decides what is separated. You choose a sieve with holes bigger than one part and smaller than the other. Sieving only works when the parts have clearly different sizes. Rava and salt are too close in size, so no kitchen sieve can part them. Shaking matters too. It gives each small piece many chances to meet a hole.
examples: At a building site, workers throw sand against a sloping wire screen. Sand falls through, and pebbles roll down the front.
A colander for washed vegetables is a sieve with large holes. Water and grit pass, and the vegetables stay.
Sieving besan before making laddu takes out the lumps.

perspectives.who: Cooks in Indian kitchens
perspectives.explanation: A cook thinks of a sieve as sorting big from small, and for round things like mustard seed and rajma that is exactly right.

perspectives.who: Engineers who test soil and sand
perspectives.explanation: They point out that a sieve measures the width of a piece and not its length. A rice grain about 6 millimetres long and 2 millimetres wide can stand on end and slip through a hole 3 millimetres across. So for long pieces, 'size' means the second smallest measurement. They stack sieves from coarse to fine to sort a soil into many sizes at once.

explanations.art: A round atta sieve held over a plate, with fine flour falling through and brown bran left on the mesh, and a zoom circle showing one hole with a small grain passing and a big flake stopped.
explanations.context: This card explains sieving and why the size of the holes must sit between the sizes of the two parts.

explanations.concept: Winnowing uses a difference in how moving air carries the parts
explanations.definition: Winnowing is separating light pieces from heavy ones by letting moving air carry the light pieces away while the heavy ones fall straight down.
explanations.description: After a paddy harvest, the grain is mixed with husk, bits of straw and dust. A farmer lifts the mixture in a flat basket and pours it slowly from shoulder height while a breeze blows. The heavy grain falls almost straight down into a heap. The light husk is blown sideways and lands farther away. The air pushes on every piece. The push moves a light, flat flake much more than a heavy, compact grain. The flat winnowing basket has many names: muram in Tamil, soop in Hindi, kulo in Bengali. At home it is flicked up and down, which tosses the mixture so that the husk flies off the front edge.
examples: Roasted peanuts rubbed between the palms shed their thin red skins. One puff of breath blows the skins away and leaves the nuts.
Blowing gently across a plate of jeera to remove dust.
Dandelion and milkweed seeds are carried off by wind while heavier seeds fall near the parent plant.

perspectives.who: Farmers across India
perspectives.explanation: They speak of light and heavy, and choose the time by the wind. Too little breeze leaves husk in the grain. Too much blows grain away with the husk.

perspectives.who: Physicists who study drag
perspectives.explanation: Drag is the push of air on a thing moving through it. They say weight alone does not decide what flies. What matters is weight compared with the area the air can push on. A husk and a grain of the same weight would still separate, because the husk is flat and wide.

explanations.art: A woman in a field pouring grain from a flat muram held high, with heavy grain falling straight into a heap and pale husk drifting sideways in the breeze.
explanations.context: This card explains a method that uses wind, which most Indian families have seen even if they have never named it.

explanations.concept: Settling and pouring off use a difference in how fast the parts sink
explanations.definition: Settling, also called sedimentation, is leaving a mixture still so that the heavier solid pieces sink to the bottom of the liquid. Pouring off the clear liquid from the top, without disturbing the bottom layer, is called decanting.
explanations.description: Wash rice in a bowl of water. Swirl it, then wait a few seconds. The rice sinks. The cloudy water above carries fine dust and loose starch, and you pour it away. You have just used settling and pouring off. Large, heavy pieces sink in seconds. Fine pieces of mud can take hours, because water drags hard on small things. Some pieces are so small that they never settle by themselves. People have long added something to help. Tiny pieces of mud that touch the helper stick together into bigger clumps, and the clumps sink.
examples: Muddy water left in a bucket overnight is clear at the top by morning, with a brown layer at the bottom.
Water works add alum, a white mineral salt, to make fine mud clump and sink before the water is filtered.
In a jar of home-made ghee, the brown milk solids settle and the clear ghee is poured off.

perspectives.who: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana chapter 45, an Indian medical text compiled by about the 4th century CE
perspectives.explanation: It lists ways to make muddy water clear. One is the seed of the kataka tree, also called the clearing nut, which is rubbed on the inside of the water pot. Another is straining through cloth. In Tamil the seed is called thettran kottai, and some families still use it.

perspectives.who: Samia Al Azharia Jahn, who studied village women's methods in Sudan in the 1970s and 1980s
perspectives.explanation: She recorded that women there cleared river water with crushed seeds of the moringa tree, the drumstick tree that came from India. Later laboratory tests showed that a protein in the seeds makes mud and many bacteria clump and sink.

perspectives.who: Water engineers
perspectives.explanation: They agree that settling removes most mud. They add that it does not remove what is dissolved, and it does not remove every microbe. So settled water still needs filtering and boiling or another treatment before drinking.

explanations.art: Three views of one glass jar of muddy water: just stirred and brown all through, after ten minutes with a layer forming, and next morning clear on top with mud at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens each time rice is washed, and names the two steps.

explanations.concept: Filtering holds back solid pieces and lets the liquid through
explanations.definition: A filter is a material with holes too small for the solid pieces to pass, such as cloth or filter paper. Filtering separates a solid that has not dissolved from a liquid. The liquid that comes through is called the filtrate, and the solid left behind is called the residue.
explanations.description: Pour tea through a strainer. The liquid runs into the cup and the leaves stay behind. A filter is a sieve for liquids, with much smaller holes. The holes in cotton cloth are too small to see easily. The holes in laboratory filter paper are about one hundredth of a millimetre across, far thinner than a hair. A filter stops only pieces bigger than its holes. Anything dissolved goes straight through with the water. Filter salty, muddy water through paper and the mud stays on the paper, but the water that drips out is still salty. That limit is important. Clear water is not always clean water.
examples: A South Indian coffee filter has two steel cups. Hot water drips through the ground coffee and through tiny holes, and the grounds stay in the top cup.
Paneer is made by pouring curdled milk through muslin. The cloth holds the solid paneer and lets the liquid whey through.
A mask filters dust out of the air you breathe.
The filter in a water purifier at home has holes small enough to stop most bacteria.

perspectives.who: Rita Colwell, Anwar Huq and their team, in villages of Bangladesh from 1999 to 2002
perspectives.explanation: They asked families to pour pond and river water through an old cotton sari folded at least four times. Cholera, a disease carried in water, fell by about half in those villages. The bacteria that cause cholera are small enough to pass through cloth. But most of them ride on larger plankton, tiny beings drifting in the water, and the folded cloth stops those.

perspectives.who: Tapputi, a perfume maker in Mesopotamia, on a clay tablet of about 1200 BCE
perspectives.explanation: The tablet records her method for making perfume for the palace. It includes straining her mixtures again and again. She is one of the first workers with materials whose name we know, and she was the overseer of the palace's perfume makers.

perspectives.who: Doctors and water engineers
perspectives.explanation: They warn that a cloth or paper filter cannot stop viruses or anything dissolved, such as salt, arsenic or fluoride. Filtering is one step. It does not make every water safe alone.

explanations.art: A funnel lined with folded filter paper over a tumbler: muddy water going in at the top, brown residue on the paper, clear drops falling, with labels 'residue' and 'filtrate'.
explanations.context: This card explains filtering, names its two products, and says plainly what a filter cannot remove.

explanations.concept: A magnet uses a difference in being attracted
explanations.definition: Magnetic separation is taking a magnetic material, such as iron or steel, out of a mixture by using a magnet, which attracts it and leaves the other materials behind.
explanations.description: Mix steel pins into a bowl of rice. Wrap a magnet in a small plastic bag and pass it through the bowl. The pins cling to the bag and the rice does not. Lift the magnet out, hold it over an empty plate and pull the magnet out of the bag. The pins drop. A magnet strongly attracts iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not attract rice, sand, plastic, wood, copper, aluminium or gold. So the method works only when one part is magnetic and the rest are not. Flour mills and spice factories pass their grain over strong magnets. A tiny chip of steel from a machine is caught before it reaches a packet.
examples: Stir a wrapped magnet through dry sand from a beach or a building site. Black grains often cling to it. They are a mineral that holds iron.
In a scrap yard, a crane with a large magnet lifts steel out of a heap of mixed scrap.

On the beaches of Chavara in Kerala and Manavalakurichi in Tamil Nadu, the sand holds valuable heavy minerals. The works there use magnets to take out ilmenite, a black mineral that is weakly attracted.

perspectives.who: School science books
perspectives.explanation: They sort materials into magnetic and non-magnetic. For choosing a separating method at home, that sorting is all you need.

perspectives.who: Physicists, since Michael Faraday's tests in 1845
perspectives.explanation: Faraday found that every material answers a strong enough magnet a little. Most are pushed or attracted so weakly that we never notice. So 'non-magnetic' means 'too weak to matter here'. Mineral works use very strong magnets to separate materials that a fridge magnet ignores.

explanations.art: A magnet inside a small plastic bag lifted from a bowl of rice with steel pins clinging to the outside of the bag.
explanations.context: This card explains separating with a magnet and reminds the reader that it works for only a few materials.

explanations.concept: Evaporation takes the water away as vapour and leaves the dissolved solid behind
explanations.definition: Evaporation is a liquid changing into a gas. When water evaporates from a solution, which is a liquid with something dissolved in it, the water leaves as water vapour and the dissolved solid stays behind.
explanations.description: Pour a little salt water into a steel plate and leave it on a sunny windowsill. In a day or two the water is gone, and a white crust is left. Taste it. It is the salt. The water did not vanish. It went into the air as water vapour, a gas you cannot see. Salt does not turn into a gas at these temperatures, so it could not follow. This is the method for a solid that has dissolved, where no filter can help. One litre of sea water holds about 35 grams of salt, which is about six level teaspoons. Evaporation gives you the solid and loses the water. To keep the water as well, the vapour must be cooled back into liquid. That longer method is called distillation.
examples: In the salt pans of Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu and the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, sea water or salty ground water is let into shallow ponds. The Sun and the wind take the water. Gujarat makes about three quarters of India's salt.

In the Salt March of 1930, Mohandas Gandhi and his companions walked about 385 kilometres to the sea at Dandi and picked up salt left by evaporated sea water. A law of the time said Indians could not make their own salt.
Jaggery is made by boiling sugarcane juice until most of the water has evaporated.
A white ring left inside a steel vessel after water has boiled away is made of minerals that were dissolved in the tap water.

perspectives.who: The Agariya families of the Little Rann of Kutch
perspectives.explanation: They have made salt there for many generations. They pump salty water from under the ground into pans they shape by treading with their feet, and rake the crystals for months in great heat. They speak of farming salt, and the knowledge of when a pan is ready is theirs.

perspectives.who: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Book 2, chapter 12, written between about 300 BCE and 300 CE
perspectives.explanation: This Indian book on running a kingdom names an officer in charge of salt, who collects the king's share from salt makers. It shows that separating salt from water was already a large, organised trade.

perspectives.who: Archaeologists, after F. R. Allchin's study of 1979
perspectives.explanation: Clay vessels found at Shaikhan Dheri in Gandhara, in today's Pakistan, look like parts of stills for distillation. They date from about 150 BCE to 350 CE. Allchin argued that distillation may have begun in ancient India. Other historians think it began in several places, and they credit Maria of Alexandria, a woman alchemist of about the 1st to 3rd century CE, with an early still.

explanations.art: A steel plate on a sunny windowsill shown twice: with a thin pool of salt water and wavy arrows of vapour rising, and later dry with white salt crystals.
explanations.context: This card explains how to get back a solid that has dissolved and cannot be filtered out.

explanations.concept: Choosing a method: find the difference, decide what you want to keep, then put the steps in order
explanations.definition: To separate a mixture of several materials, list the parts, find one difference for each part, pick the method that uses that difference, and do the dry methods before the wet ones.
explanations.description: Think of a mixture of steel pins, rajma, sand and salt. No single method can part all four. So you use a chain. First, pass a magnet through it. Only the pins come out. Second, sieve it. The rajma stays on the sieve, and the sand and salt fall through. Third, add water and stir. The salt dissolves and the sand does not. Fourth, filter. The sand stays on the paper. Fifth, evaporate the water. The salt comes back. The order matters. A magnet and a sieve work best on dry things, so they come before the water. You also ask what you want to keep. If you want only the sand, you can pour the salty water away and skip the last step.
examples: Rava and salt, the puzzle at the start: add water, filter through cloth so the rava stays, then evaporate the water to get the salt.
Tea leaves, sugar and water in a cup of black tea: a strainer takes the leaves, and evaporation would bring back the sugar.
Muddy water: let it settle, pour off the top, then filter what you poured.

perspectives.who: Chemists in a laboratory
perspectives.explanation: They choose the method that gives the purest part, even if it is slow, because their tests need clean materials.

perspectives.who: Engineers at a factory, a mine or a water works
perspectives.explanation: They choose by cost. Each step uses energy, water, time and people's work. They often accept a part that is clean enough and not perfect. They also ask where the unwanted part will go, because it does not disappear.

perspectives.who: Groups that work on waste, such as Hasiru Dala in Bengaluru
perspectives.explanation: They say the cheapest separation is the one you never have to do. Wet waste and dry waste kept in two bins at home need no separating later.

explanations.art: A flow chart of five boxes joined by arrows (magnet, sieve, add water, filter, evaporate), with a small picture under each box of the part that leaves at that step.
explanations.context: This card brings the methods together and shows how to plan a separation with more than one step.

explanations.concept: Chromatography separates materials that differ only a little, such as the colours in one ink
explanations.definition: Chromatography is a method in which a liquid creeps through paper or powder and carries the parts of a mixture along at different speeds, so that they spread out into separate bands.
explanations.description: Draw a thick dot with a black sketch pen near the bottom of a strip of filter paper or a white coffee filter. Dip only the bottom edge in water. The water climbs the paper and passes through the dot. As it climbs, the black spreads into bands of blue, pink or yellow. Many black inks are a mixture of dyes. Each dye differs a little in how strongly it clings to the paper and how well it dissolves in water. A dye that clings less travels farther. So a small difference, repeated over the whole climb, becomes a gap you can see. Chromatography is used wherever the parts are too alike for a sieve or a filter.
examples: Laboratories use it to check food for colours that are not allowed.
Sports bodies use a form of it to test athletes' samples for banned drugs.
A permanent marker does not spread in water. Its dyes dissolve in spirit and not in water, so a different liquid is needed.

perspectives.who: Mikhail Tsvet, a botanist working in Warsaw, in 1903
perspectives.explanation: He washed an extract of green leaves down a glass tube packed with chalk powder. The green separated into bands of green and yellow. Leaf green was a mixture of several pigments, which are coloured materials. He named the method chromatography, from Greek words for colour and writing.

perspectives.who: Archer Martin and Richard Synge, in 1941
perspectives.explanation: For about thirty years few chemists used Tsvet's method. Martin and Synge worked out why it separates and made it work for colourless materials too. Since then it has become one of the most used methods in chemistry.

explanations.art: A strip of white paper standing in a shallow dish of water, with a black dot near the bottom that has spread upward into separate blue, pink and yellow bands.
explanations.context: This card shows that the idea of using a difference still works when the difference is very small.

explanations.concept: Living beings separate mixtures all day, using the same differences
explanations.definition: Every living being takes what they need out of a mixture, such as air, water or food, and leaves or sends back the rest. Bodies do this with filters, with evaporation and with surfaces that let some materials through and stop others.
explanations.description: You are separating a mixture as you read this. The air you breathe in is about 21 parts oxygen in every 100. The air you breathe out is about 16. Your lungs took some oxygen out of the mixture and left the rest. Your two kidneys filter your blood. About 180 litres of liquid pass through their filters each day. The kidneys take back nearly all of it and send out about one and a half litres as urine. Every cell does the same on a small scale. A cell's skin lets some materials in and keeps others out. A cell chooses what to let in. Many biologists describe this as automatic chemistry, with no choosing in it.
examples: A flamingo feeds with their head upside down. Their beak has rows of fine plates like a comb. Their tongue pumps water in and out, and the plates hold back tiny algae and small animals.
Honey bees collect nectar, which can be more than half water. In the hive they spread it thin and fan it with their wings until enough water has evaporated. Honey is under one fifth water.
An oyster draws sea water across their gills and filters out floating food. One adult oyster can filter more than 100 litres in a day.
A mangrove tree of the Sundarbans takes in salty water. Their roots stop most of the salt, and some kinds push the rest out through their leaves.

perspectives.who: Physiologists, who study how bodies work
perspectives.explanation: They describe a kidney or a gill by its sizes, pressures and flows, and can build a machine that copies it. A dialysis machine filters the blood of a person whose kidneys have stopped working.

perspectives.who: Biologists who study how cells sense and respond, such as the microbiologist James Shapiro
perspectives.explanation: They describe cells as sensing what is around them and acting on it. A bacterium detects sugar outside, makes the right gate in their skin and lets the sugar in. In this view, separating is something a living being does, and is a form of deciding.

explanations.art: A flamingo feeding with head upside down in shallow water, with a zoom circle of the comb-like plates in the beak holding back tiny green specks while water flows out.
explanations.context: This card shows that separating mixtures is not only a human skill: bodies and cells do it to stay alive.

explanations.concept: The Earth separates mixtures too: rain, rivers and salt lakes
explanations.definition: Sunlight, moving water, wind and gravity separate the Earth's materials by the same differences people use: evaporation leaves salt behind, and flowing water sorts stones by size.
explanations.description: The sea is salty and rain is not. The Sun warms the sea and water evaporates. The salt cannot follow, so the vapour that makes clouds is fresh. Rain is sea water that the Sun has separated. Rivers sort too. A fast mountain stream can roll large stones. As the river slows on the plain, it drops the pebbles first, then the sand, then the silt. The finest clay travels to the delta. So a river lays out its load by size, as a stack of sieves would. Where a lake has no way out to the sea, water leaves only by evaporation. The salts stay and build up year after year.
examples: Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is India's largest salt lake away from the coast. Rivers flow in, no river flows out, and people have collected salt there for well over a thousand years.
The Ganga carries boulders near Rishikesh, sand through the plains and fine silt to the Sundarbans delta.
Wind blowing across a beach carries the fine, light sand inland to build dunes and leaves the coarse shell pieces behind.

perspectives.who: Geologists
perspectives.explanation: They read the sizes of grains in a rock to tell how fast the water was moving when the grains were laid down. Sorting by a river that dried up long ago is still recorded in stone.

perspectives.who: Chandogya Upanishad, 6.10
perspectives.explanation: The text says that the rivers flow east and west and enter the sea. The sea's water rises as cloud and falls as rain, and it is all one sea. Once joined, the rivers do not know 'I am this river' or 'I am that river'. The sage uses the water's journey to speak of all beings sharing one ground.

explanations.art: A side view from mountains to sea: a river dropping boulders, then pebbles, then sand, then fine mud at the delta, with vapour rising from the sea to a cloud and rain falling on the mountains.
explanations.context: This card shows the lesson's methods happening on the scale of the whole Earth, with no person doing them.

explanations.concept: Some mixtures look like one material: air, sea water, milk, steel and gold jewellery
explanations.definition: In a uniform mixture, the parts are spread so evenly and are so small that the mixture looks the same all through. Scientists call this a homogeneous mixture. A mixture whose different parts you can see is called heterogeneous.
explanations.description: A plate of bhel puri is plainly a mixture. You can see the puffed rice, the onion and the sev. A glass of salt water is a mixture too, but your eyes see one clear liquid. The parts are single particles, far too small to see. Air is the same. Dry air is about 78 parts nitrogen, 21 parts oxygen and 1 part argon in every 100, with a very small amount of carbon dioxide. No part of a room has its own patch of oxygen. So looking is not a safe test for a mixture. You need another test. Tasting found the salt. Evaporation would find it too.
examples: Gold jewellery marked 916 is 22-carat gold. It is 916 parts gold in every 1,000. The rest is copper, silver or zinc, mixed in to make the gold hard enough to wear.
Milk looks like one white liquid. Under a microscope it is water with tiny floating drops of fat. Churning curd gathers that fat into butter.
A steel tumbler is iron mixed with chromium, nickel and a little carbon.
Mist is tiny drops of water mixed into air.

perspectives.who: Shoppers and cooks
perspectives.explanation: We call air, milk and steel by one name each and treat each as one material. For cooking, breathing and buying a tumbler, that works.

perspectives.who: Chemists
perspectives.explanation: They ask how small the mixed pieces are. In a solution such as salt water, the pieces are single particles. In milk and mist the pieces are larger clumps, still too small for the eye, and this kind of mixture is called a colloid. In bhel puri the pieces are easy to see.

explanations.art: Four pictures in a row (a plate of bhel puri, a glass of milk, a glass of salt water, a gold bangle stamped 916), each with a zoom circle showing the parts inside.
explanations.context: This card warns that many things we call by one name are mixtures, and that eyes alone cannot tell.

explanations.concept: How pure is 'pure'? Purity is a number, and it is never quite 100
explanations.definition: A pure material is made of one substance only. In practice no sample is perfectly pure, so purity is given as a number that says how much of the sample is the named substance.
explanations.description: A packet says 'pure salt'. A bottle says 'pure water'. In a shop, pure means clean and safe, with nothing added that should not be there. A chemist means something stricter: one substance and nothing else. By that meaning, hardly anything you have touched is pure. Bottled drinking water has minerals dissolved in it, and the label lists them. The purest gold bars are stamped 999, which means 999 parts gold in 1,000. The silicon used for computer chips is among the purest materials people make. Its makers reach about 99.9999999 parts in 100. That is one stray atom among a hundred crore, and still not zero. Each cleaner grade costs more work than the last.
examples: Table salt often has a little iodine added on purpose, to keep people healthy. It is a mixture by design.
Rainwater has dissolved gases from the air and dust that the drops formed around.
Water with nearly everything removed is used in laboratories and chip factories. It is a poor carrier of electricity.

perspectives.who: Indian food safety rules and shop labels
perspectives.explanation: Here 'pure' is a promise that nothing harmful or cheap has been mixed in. Pure ghee means no vanaspati has been added. The word is about trust between a seller and a buyer.

perspectives.who: Chemists
perspectives.explanation: They never write 'pure' without a number. They give a grade, such as 99.9 in 100, and say which test measured it. A better instrument can find a smaller trace, so the number depends on how closely anyone has looked.

perspectives.who: Anaxagoras, in Greece, about 450 BCE, in the fragments numbered 6 and 11
perspectives.explanation: He taught that in everything there is a portion of everything. A thing is named after what it has most of. He reasoned this from food: bread and water somehow become hair and bone, so he held that hair and bone must already be in them in small amounts. Chemists today explain that change differently, by materials being rebuilt in the body.

explanations.art: A gold bar stamped 999, a bottle of drinking water with its mineral label enlarged, and a silicon disc, each with a tiny dot marked 'the rest'.
explanations.context: This card looks hard at the word 'pure' and shows that it means different things in a shop and in a laboratory.

explanations.concept: Is water just H2O? Even one 'pure' substance is a mixture on a closer look
explanations.definition: Scientists and philosophers disagree about whether water is one substance, or a mixture of several kinds of water molecules that differ slightly.
explanations.description: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. School books say that water is one substance, made of molecules written H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Take water with every other material removed. Look closer, and it still holds a mixture. Hydrogen atoms come in a common light kind and a rare heavy kind. So about 1 water molecule in every 3,200 has one heavy hydrogen atom and weighs more. At any moment, about 2 molecules in every 100 crore have split into two charged pieces. The molecules also cling to each other in groups that form and break very quickly. So is water one thing, or a mixture of kinds? Scientists and philosophers of science do not agree. What would you count as 'the same kind'?
examples: Heavy water, in which both hydrogen atoms are the heavy kind, can be separated from ordinary water. India makes it in special plants for some of its nuclear power stations.
Ice made of heavy water sinks in ordinary water, while ordinary ice floats.

perspectives.who: Most chemistry books
perspectives.explanation: Water is the substance whose molecules are H2O. The heavy kind and the split pieces are small details of that one substance. This view lets chemists name materials simply and it works for nearly every task.

perspectives.who: The philosopher of science Michael Weisberg, in 'Water is not H2O', 2006
perspectives.explanation: He argues that the formula alone does not pick out what we call water. What counts as the same substance depends on what you are doing. For drinking, heavy and light water are different, because a large amount of heavy water harms a body. For many other tasks they are the same.

perspectives.who: The historian and philosopher of science Hasok Chang, in 'Is Water H2O?', 2012
perspectives.explanation: He shows that chemists argued for decades in the 1800s before settling on the formula, and that other systems also fitted the evidence of the time. He asks us to hold the formula as a very successful way of describing water, and to keep other ways of describing in view.

explanations.art: A drop of water with a zoom circle showing many identical small molecules, one drawn slightly bigger and darker and labelled 'heavy', and two broken pieces with plus and minus signs.
explanations.context: This card takes the question of purity as far down as it goes and shows that the answer depends on what we count as the same.

explanations.concept: Mixing happens by itself, but separating always needs work
explanations.definition: Materials that can mix will spread into each other if left alone. Taking them apart again always needs energy, from the Sun, a fire, a motor or a body.
explanations.description: Let one drop of blue ink fall into a tumbler of still water. Do not stir. In an hour the whole tumbler is pale blue. The ink mixed itself in, because the particles of water and ink never stop moving. Now wait for the ink to gather back into a drop. You can wait for ever. To get it out you must do something, such as evaporating all the water, and that takes energy. Every method in this lesson has such a cost. Your arm shakes the sieve. The Sun dries the salt pan. Getting drinking water from the sea shows the size of the cost. The best plants use about 3 to 4 units of electricity for every 1,000 litres. Physics sets a lowest possible cost of about 1 unit, and no machine can go below it.
examples: The Minjur plant near Chennai, opened in 2010, makes about 10 crore litres of drinking water from sea water each day, and uses a great deal of electricity to do it.
The smell of agarbatti spreads through a room without a fan. Nobody has seen the smell gather back into the stick.
Your kidneys use about one tenth of the energy your body spends at rest, mostly to take back salts and water after filtering.

perspectives.who: Engineers
perspectives.explanation: They treat the cost of separating as a bill to be cut. Much of the energy used by the world's factories goes into separating things: metals from rock, petrol from crude oil, fresh water from salt water.

perspectives.who: Physicists, since Rudolf Clausius in 1865
perspectives.explanation: They measure how spread out and mixed things are with a number called entropy. Left alone, the entropy of a closed box of things goes up or stays the same. Separating lowers the entropy in one place, and it always raises it by more somewhere else, usually as waste heat.

explanations.art: Three tumblers in a row: a blue drop just entering clear water, the blue spreading in threads, and the whole tumbler pale blue, with a crossed-out arrow pointing back from the third to the first.
explanations.context: This card explains why unmixing is so much harder than mixing, with a real number for the cost.

explanations.concept: Why does mixing go only one way? Science has a partial answer and then runs out
explanations.definition: Physicists can explain why mixed arrangements are far more likely than separated ones. They cannot yet explain why the universe started in an orderly state, which is what gives the world a 'before' and an 'after'.
explanations.description: Here is the puzzle. Film two particles bumping and play the film backwards. Nothing looks wrong. The rules for single particles work the same both ways in time. Now film ink spreading in water and play it backwards. Everyone can tell it is backwards. In 1877 Ludwig Boltzmann gave a reason. There are hugely more ways for ink particles to be spread out than gathered in one drop. Moving at random, they almost surely end up spread out. But that reason needs a start. The ink had to begin as a drop. Follow that back, and the whole universe had to begin very orderly. Nobody knows why it did. Science also has no agreed definition of time itself. What do you think makes 'before' different from 'after'?
examples: Shuffle a new pack of cards that is in order. It becomes mixed. Keep shuffling a mixed pack and it almost never returns to order, because the mixed orders hugely outnumber the sorted ones.
Hot tea and cold milk make warm tea. Warm tea never sorts itself into a hot half and a cold half.

perspectives.who: Ludwig Boltzmann, in 1877
perspectives.explanation: Mixing is a matter of chance and counting. Unmixing by itself is not forbidden. It is so unlikely for a tumbler of water that it would not be seen once in many lifetimes of the universe.

perspectives.who: Josef Loschmidt, in 1876
perspectives.explanation: He objected that if every particle's motion were exactly turned round, the ink would gather again. So the rules alone cannot explain the one-way direction. Something about how things start must be added.

perspectives.who: The philosopher David Albert and the physicist Roger Penrose
perspectives.explanation: They hold that the answer lies at the beginning of the universe, which was in a very special orderly state. Albert named this the past hypothesis. Why the beginning was like that is unknown. Some physicists, such as Carlo Rovelli, add that time may not be a basic part of the world at all.

explanations.art: A film strip of an ink drop spreading in water, with a second strip below showing the same frames in reverse order and a large question mark between them.
explanations.context: This card says plainly what science can explain about one-way mixing and where it has no answer.

explanations.concept: Is 'mixed' a fact about the materials, or about what a test can tell apart?
explanations.definition: Scientists disagree about whether two materials count as mixed because of what they are, or only because we have a test that can tell them apart.
explanations.description: Take two tumblers of water, one coloured red and one blue. Pour them together. They mix into purple, and you cannot easily get them back. Now take two tumblers of the same plain water and pour them together. Did mixing happen? The molecules from the two tumblers have spread among each other in just the same way. Yet no test can find any change. In the 1870s the American scientist Josiah Willard Gibbs noticed something odd in the sums. When two different gases mix, the entropy, the number that measures mixing, jumps up. The jump is the same size however small the difference between the gases. When the gases are the same, the jump is zero. So mixing seems to depend on whether a difference can be told. What do you think?
examples: Mix white rice from two different bags of the same kind. Nobody would call the result a mixture, unless they had a test that could tell the bags apart.
Before the heavy kind of hydrogen was found in 1931, a jar of water counted as one substance. Afterwards the same jar could be described as a mixture.

perspectives.who: The physicist Edwin Jaynes, in 'The Gibbs Paradox', 1992
perspectives.explanation: He argued that entropy is not a property of the material alone. It depends on which differences we have chosen, or are able, to keep track of. Find a new way to tell two things apart, and what was one material becomes a mixture that can be separated.

perspectives.who: Many physicists who work with quantum physics
perspectives.explanation: They answer that in quantum physics two particles of the same kind are exactly alike, with no hidden label at all. So whether two gases are the same or different is a plain fact about the world, and it needs no watcher. Here 'watcher' means any test or instrument, and not a mind.

perspectives.who: The Jain teaching of anekantavada, set out by Siddhasena Divakara in the Sanmati Tarka, about the 5th century CE
perspectives.explanation: This teaching holds that a thing has many sides, and each statement about it is true from one standpoint. From the standpoint of what the parts are, the two tumblers of water are one. From the standpoint of where each part came from, they are two.

explanations.art: Two pairs of tumblers: red and blue poured into one purple tumbler labelled 'mixed', and two clear tumblers poured into one clear tumbler labelled 'mixed?'.
explanations.context: This card asks a question that scientists still argue about: who or what decides that two things are different enough to be a mixture.

explanations.concept: Joining and parting in old Indian thought: samyoga and vibhaga
explanations.definition: In the Vaisheshika school of Indian philosophy, samyoga means the coming together of things and vibhaga means their coming apart. The school taught that all the things we see are made and unmade by these two.
explanations.description: The Vaisheshika thinkers asked what the world is made of. Their answer was tiny particles, called paramanu, that cannot be cut further. On their account, the things we see are made when particles come together, and end when particles come apart. The particles themselves are not made or destroyed. That is close to what this lesson found with rice and dal: the parts stay themselves through mixing and separating. The old thinkers reached their view by reasoning. They did no experiments of the kind chemists do, and their particles are not the atoms of modern science. The old Indian thinkers also disagreed with each other about what a combined thing is. What would you ask them?
examples: Tradition says the founder of the school was called Kanada, which can mean 'grain eater', because he lived on grains gathered from the fields after harvest.
A clay pot, in the Vaisheshika account, is a new whole that exists while its particles stay joined, and ends when they part.

perspectives.who: Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutra, 1.1.6, composed between about the 6th and 2nd centuries BCE
perspectives.explanation: The sutra lists the qualities a thing can have. Among them are separateness, joining (samyoga) and parting (vibhaga), beside colour, taste and smell. So for this school, being joined to another thing is a quality, as real as being red.

perspectives.who: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 5 (verse 5.33 in a common numbering), a Jain text of about the 2nd to 5th century CE
perspectives.explanation: It says that particles of matter bind together because of two opposite qualities, which the text calls smooth and rough. Some modern readers compare this with positive and negative charge. That is a comparison made today, and the text does not describe electric charge.

perspectives.who: The Milindapanha, Book 2, chapter 1, a Buddhist text of about the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE
perspectives.explanation: The monk Nagasena asks King Milinda if a chariot is the wheels, the axle or the pole. It is none of them. 'Chariot' is a name used when the parts are together. On this Buddhist view, a combined thing is only a name. The Vaisheshika school held the opposite: a whole is a new real thing over and above its parts.

explanations.art: A palm-leaf manuscript page beside a drawing of small dots coming together to form a clay pot and drifting apart again.
explanations.context: This card gives the views of old Indian schools on what joining and parting are, and says honestly how they differ from modern chemistry and from each other.

agreed.text: The Earth itself is sorted by density: the heaviest material is at the centre and the lightest is on top.
agreed.evidence: Surface rocks weigh about 3 grams for each cubic centimetre, but the whole Earth averages about 5.5. So the inside must be much denser. Earthquake waves bend and bounce at layers deep down. In 1936 the Danish scientist Inge Lehmann used such waves to show a solid inner core inside the liquid outer core. Both are mostly iron, which sank when the young Earth was molten.

agreed.text: Spinning a mixture fast separates parts by density much more quickly than settling does.
agreed.evidence: A machine called a centrifuge spins a tube of blood for a few minutes. The red cells, which are denser, collect at the bottom and take up a little under half the tube. A pale yellow liquid called plasma stays on top. Dairies separate cream from milk in the same way. Churning curd with a wooden mathu to gather butter is an older use of spinning.

agreed.text: Plastic that has broken into tiny pieces is now mixed into the sea, the soil, the air and living bodies, and nobody has a practical way to take it out.
agreed.evidence: In 2004 Richard Thompson and his team reported tiny plastic fibres and fragments in beach sand and in old plankton samples from around Britain, and named them microplastics. Since then they have been found in deep-sea mud, mountain snow, table salt and human blood. Filters can catch them in a factory pipe, but not across an ocean.

agreed.text: Crude oil is separated into petrol, kerosene, diesel and tar by boiling, because each part turns to gas at a different temperature.
agreed.evidence: In a refinery, heated oil vapour rises up a tall tower that is cooler towards the top. Each part turns back to liquid at its own height and is piped off. Refineries such as the ones at Jamnagar, Kochi and Digboi work this way. Digboi in Assam has run since 1901.

agreed.text: The gases of air can be separated by cooling air until it becomes liquid.
agreed.evidence: Air cooled to about 200 degrees below zero Celsius becomes a pale blue liquid. As it warms a little, nitrogen boils off first and oxygen later. Carl von Linde built the first plant to do this in 1895. The oxygen cylinders in hospitals are filled from such plants.

challenging.claim: In a sea-water filter, water does not flow through tiny holes. It dissolves into the sheet and moves through it one molecule at a time.
challenging.who: Harry Lonsdale, Ulrich Merten and Robert Riley in 1965, for the dissolving view. Li Wang, Menachem Elimelech and their team, in Science Advances in 2023, for the tiny-holes view.
challenging.for: The dissolving view has matched the measured flow of water and salt for nearly sixty years, and engineers have designed working plants with it.
challenging.against: The 2023 team ran computer models of the sheet, atom by atom, and did new tests. They report that water moves in connected clusters through passages that open between the plastic chains, pushed by pressure, as it would through holes. Other groups are still checking this.
challenging.context: Sea water is made drinkable by pushing it through a thin plastic sheet that passes water and stops most salt. Millions of people drink this water, and scientists still argue about how the sheet works.

challenging.claim: A mixture is nothing more than its parts. If you know the parts fully, you know everything about the whole.
challenging.who: Many physicists and chemists hold this view, called reductionism. The physicist Philip Anderson argued against it in 'More Is Different', Science, 1972.
challenging.for: Taking things apart has explained a great deal. The saltiness of sea water, the hardness of steel and the colours of ink were each understood by finding the parts.
challenging.against: Anderson pointed out that large groups of particles show behaviour, such as wetness or forming a crystal, that makes no sense for one particle. Each level needs its own ideas. Nobody has yet worked out a living cell's behaviour from a list of its molecules.
challenging.context: This lesson showed that parts keep their properties in a mixture. It also showed that salt water does things neither salt nor water does. So is the whole only its parts?

challenging.claim: Crushed moringa seeds can clean drinking water as well as the chemicals used in a water works.
challenging.who: Samia Al Azharia Jahn recorded the practice of Sudanese village women and tested it from the 1970s. Stephanie Velegol and Darrell Velegol's team, from 2010, studied how the seed protein works.
challenging.for: Tests show the seeds remove most of the mud and a large share of the bacteria. The tree grows across India and Africa and the seeds cost almost nothing.
challenging.against: The seeds leave plant material in the water, and bacteria can grow again on it within a day. The seeds do not remove dissolved poisons such as arsenic. Most water engineers say the treated water must be used the same day and is still safer after boiling.
challenging.context: An old way of clearing water, kept alive mostly by women, has been tested in laboratories. It works, with limits that are still being measured.

challenging.claim: Water keeps a memory of a material that was once dissolved in it, even after so much thinning with more water that none of the material is left.
challenging.who: The French scientist Jacques Benveniste and his team, in Nature in 1988. The claim is used to support homeopathy.
challenging.for: Benveniste's laboratory reported that a solution thinned until no molecule of the active material should remain still acted on blood cells.
challenging.against: A team sent by the journal watched the tests repeated with the tubes secretly relabelled, so that nobody knew which was which. The effect disappeared. Later attempts by other laboratories did not find it. The groups that water molecules form last for less than a billionth of a second.
challenging.context: This claim is about what remains after separating. It is here because it was tested fairly and openly, which is how science is meant to treat a surprising idea.

big_questions.q: Sugar stirred into tea has lost its shape, its crunch and its white colour, and kept only its sweetness. How many of its properties can a material lose and still be the same material?
big_questions.hint: List what changed and what came back when the water was evaporated. Then ask which properties you would use to recognise sugar.

big_questions.q: A sieve cannot separate two grains of exactly the same size. Suppose two things had no difference at all that any test could find. Would putting them together make a mixture?
big_questions.hint: Think about pouring two tumblers of the same water together. Then think about what might be found with a better instrument a hundred years from now.

big_questions.q: When you clean rice, the stones are the unwanted part. For someone building a path, the stones are the wanted part. Who decides which part of a mixture is the rubbish?
big_questions.hint: Think of rice-washing water given to plants, husk fed to cattle, and what a flamingo wants from a salt pan.

big_questions.q: Ink mixes into water without any help, and it never unmixes without help. The rules for single particles work both ways. So where does the one-way direction come from?
big_questions.hint: Count how many ways the ink could be spread out and how many ways it could be in one drop. Then ask how the ink came to be in a drop to begin with.

big_questions.q: Your body is a mixture of water, salts, fats, proteins and air, and the atoms in it are swapped for new ones all the time. If every material in you were separated and laid in jars on a table, where would you be?
big_questions.hint: Ask what is missing from the jars that was there before. Is it a material, an arrangement, or something else?

big_questions.q: Is it fairer to mix waste and pay someone to separate it later, or to keep it apart from the start? Who does the work in each case, and who gets the benefit?
big_questions.hint: Think about who handles a mixed dustbin after it leaves your home, and what that work is like.

big_questions.q: Is there anything in the world that is not a mixture? If you thought you had found one, how could you ever prove it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each test can and cannot find, and whether passing every test known today is the same as being pure.

big_questions.q: A child joins a new class, or a family moves to a new city. Do people keep their own properties in a group, as rice does in dal, or do they change, as milk does with lemon?
big_questions.hint: Think of something about you that stays the same everywhere, and something that is different with different people.

big_questions.q: A cell stays alive by keeping the mixture inside different from the mixture outside. Is a living being a thing that separates, or is being alive the separating itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a kidney, a root and a cell's skin are doing every second, and what happens to a body when that work stops.

open_questions.q: Why did the universe begin in such an orderly state that things have been mixing ever since?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can explain why mixing is likely once you start from order. No accepted theory explains the orderly start. It may need a theory of the beginning of the universe, or of what time is, and neither exists yet.

open_questions.q: How does water really pass through the thin plastic sheet that takes salt out of sea water?
open_questions.why_open: The passages in the sheet are about the size of a few water molecules and keep changing shape. No microscope can watch water move through them. Computer models and flow measurements point to two different pictures, and tests to decide between them are still being done.

open_questions.q: Can carbon dioxide be taken back out of the air at a cost the world can pay?
open_questions.why_open: Carbon dioxide is only about 4 parts in every 10,000 of air, so a machine must handle a huge amount of air to catch a little. Physics sets a lowest energy cost, and today's machines use several times that. Trees, soils and seas already do this work, and how best to help them is also argued over.

open_questions.q: How did the first cells come to keep their inside different from their outside?
open_questions.why_open: A living cell needs a skin that lets some materials in and keeps others out. Fatty molecules can form such bubbles by themselves in water, as laboratory tests show. How a bubble first came to hold the right mixture and to control what crossed its skin is not known, because no trace of those first cells is left.

open_questions.q: Can the behaviour of a whole mixture, such as a living cell, be worked out from its parts alone?
open_questions.why_open: For a simple mixture such as salt water, chemists can now predict much from the parts. For a cell, with thousands of kinds of molecules acting on each other, nobody can. Scientists disagree on whether this is only a matter of bigger computers or whether wholes need ideas of their own.

open_questions.q: How can the tiny pieces of plastic now mixed into the sea and the soil be removed, or will they stay?
open_questions.why_open: The pieces are spread thinly through enormous amounts of water and soil, and many are the same size as living plankton, so a filter that catches the plastic also catches living beings. Some bacteria and fungi can break down a few plastics slowly. Whether that can work outside a laboratory is being tested.

story.title: What Everyone Took from the Sea
story.note: A made-up story set at the salt pans near Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu. The people are imagined. What is real: sea water is led through a row of ponds as it dries, a chalky mineral called gypsum comes out of the water before the eating salt does, a bitter liquid called bittern is left at the end, and factories take other salts from it. Flamingos do feed in these salt pans on brine shrimp and algae, and a flamingo's pink colour comes from that food.
text: Before sunrise the salt pans outside Thoothukudi lay grey and flat, like a hundred slates set side by side. Thenmozhi, who was nine, walked along the mud bank behind her mother, Selvi, carrying the short wooden rake. Behind her came Joseph, the neighbour's son, who was seven and had never been to the pans before.
Joseph looked all round. 'Where is the factory?' he asked. 'Where does the salt get made?'
Thenmozhi laughed. 'Nobody makes it.'

'The sea makes it,' said a voice. It was Pechiammal paatti, the oldest worker on the pans, already bent over her square of white. 'We sow sea water after Pongal, and we reap in the hot months. The salt grows, child, as paddy grows. It is a crop.'
'It does not grow, paatti,' said Thenmozhi. 'We learnt it. The salt was in the sea water all the time. The Sun only takes the water away.'
Paatti did not stop raking. 'Then tell me this. The same sea water stands in that big pond over there. Why is there no salt in it? Why does it come only here, in my pan?'
Thenmozhi opened her mouth and found she did not know.

Selvi answered for neither of them. She led the children to the first pond, wide and deep to the ankle. 'Taste.' It tasted like the sea. 'Here the water can still hold all its salt. Every day the Sun takes a little water. The salt stays, so the same salt is crowded into less and less water.' She walked them along the bank to a middle pond and scraped the floor with her heel. A grey-white crust came up. 'This comes out first. It is not for eating. A man from the plaster works buys it. It lets go of the water before the salt does.' Then she brought them back to paatti's pan, where crystals lay like broken glass. 'Only here is the water so crowded that it cannot hold the eating salt any longer. So here the salt shows itself.'
'And after?' asked Joseph. A little brown water was left in the corner of the pan. He dipped a finger and licked it, and his whole face folded. It was bitter.
'That we drain away,' said Selvi. 'A truck comes for it some months. A factory takes other salts out of it.'
Out in the middle pond stood a line of flamingos, heads upside down in the water, swinging slowly from side to side.
'What are they taking?' Joseph asked.
'Tiny shrimp, and green specks smaller than the shrimp,' said Selvi. 'Their beak is a comb. The water goes out through the comb and the food stays in.'
'Do they want the salt?'
'They cannot stand the salt. They push it out again. To them the salt is the rubbish.'

Joseph counted on his fingers. 'The Sun took the water. The plaster man takes the grey crust. You take the salt. The factory takes the bitter water. The flamingos take the shrimp.' He looked up. 'So what is left that nobody wants?'
Nobody could name anything.

Thenmozhi was quiet. At school the word had been 'impurities': the part you throw away. But here each one who came to the pond called a different part the prize, and called the rest waste. The pond did not seem to have an opinion.
'So who is right, kanna?' said paatti, straightening her back at last. 'Did the sea give me a crop? Or was your salt sitting there all the time?'

Thenmozhi thought about it properly. The salt had been in the sea. That was true. But in the sea it had no whiteness, no edges and no crunch. It had only a taste. And without the ponds, the waiting, and paatti carrying it on her head, not one crystal would ever have reached a plate.
'I think both,' she said slowly. 'It was there. And it was not salt you could hold until you did this.'
Paatti made a small sound that might have been a laugh.

The Sun came over the edge of the pans. The flamingos lifted all at once, and their wings opened pink against the grey. Selvi had once said that the pink came from their food. So the pink had been in the pond too, spread through the water in specks too small to see, until a bird gathered enough of it to show.
Thenmozhi looked down at the dull water by her feet. She wondered what else was in there that nobody had found a way to gather yet.
story.epiphany: A separation adds nothing. It only lets one part leave, by a difference that part already had. Which part is the prize and which is the waste is decided by whoever is doing the separating.
ask: Paatti says the salt is a crop that grows. Thenmozhi says it was in the sea all the time. What is true in each way of saying it?
The flamingos treat salt as rubbish and the salt workers treat it as the prize. Can you think of a mixture at home where your rubbish is someone else's prize?
The salt in the sea had a taste but no shape. Was it already salt?
What do you think is in a glass of your tap water that nobody has looked for yet? How would you look?
