how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most thinkers in Greece, India and elsewhere counted air as one single element. It fitted what everyone saw. Air has no colour, no smell and no parts that anyone could pick out. In the 1770s three people broke it open. Carl Scheele in Sweden and Joseph Priestley in England each made a gas in which a candle burned brighter. In Paris, Antoine Lavoisier showed that this gas, oxygen, is about one fifth of air, and that the rest does not keep a flame alive. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier translated the English papers for him, drew the apparatus and kept the records of the tests. So air was a mixture of two gases. For a century that seemed complete. Then in 1892 Lord Rayleigh weighed nitrogen taken from air and nitrogen made from chemicals. The nitrogen from air was heavier by about one part in 200. He and William Ramsay hunted for the reason. In 1894 they found a third gas hiding in air, about 1 part in 100, and named it argon. A tiny difference in weight had shown a part that nobody had looked for.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Wilhelm Scheele, Joseph Priestley, Antoine Lavoisier, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt), William Ramsay
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Air is one single pure element, with no parts.

roots.context: You have taken mixtures apart with a sieve, a magnet, a filter and the Sun. Now we ask what mixing and separating tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You filtered muddy salt water, and it came out clear. To your eyes it was plain water. Then you let it dry, and salt was left on the plate. The filter paper found no second material, and evaporation found one. So 'pure' tells you which tests a thing has passed, and a new test can still find more.
deep_truth.habit: We call clear water, white salt or a gold bangle 'pure', as if purity were something the material has, like its weight. That label hides the fact that it only records the tests used so far. It makes each thing look single and closed, when a closer test keeps finding other things in it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the mud, salt and water test, the filtrate looked as clear as plain water, yet a white crust of salt was left when it dried. Air was called one element for two thousand years, until a difference of one part in 200 in weight showed argon in it.

three.who_am_i: You are a mixture that keeps changing. The water you drank this morning is part of you now, and some of the air in your lungs was outside the window a minute ago. No test finds a hard line where the world stops and you begin. So asking 'who am I?' means asking what stays when every part is being swapped.
three.what_is_life: A stone lets the world mix with it as it comes. A living cell keeps choosing: this in, that out. A being is alive for as long as they keep the mixture inside different from the mixture outside. So life is a way of separating that never stops, done by every being from a bacterium to a banyan.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea becomes cloud, the cloud becomes rain, the rain carries salt back to the sea. Nothing separated ever leaves the world. It only moves to another place in it. Every part you can pull out of a mixture was part of one whole before, and is part of one whole after.

roots.thread: Every method in this lesson worked because the parts were different. So separating is how we come to know differences. But each time, the difference was found and not made: the salt was salty before the plate dried. And each cleaner part turned out, on a closer test, to hold other things again. Follow that down and no part is ever found standing completely alone. Consciousness is the ground that all these parts arise from, and the many materials are that one ground showing itself in different ways. Many scientists do not accept this last step, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put a lump of salt in water and bring it back in the morning. The salt cannot be found. The son sips from the top, the middle and the bottom, and every sip is salty. The teacher says that the finest essence of everything is present like that, unseen and all through, and adds: you are that.
teachings.link: The lesson did the same test. A dissolved solid is in every drop though no eye and no filter finds it, and only tasting or drying shows it. The sage then takes a step that science does not take: from salt in water to one essence in all beings.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at a hub, and the cart is useful because of the empty hole at the centre. Clay is shaped into a pot, and the pot is useful because of the empty space inside. What is there gives a thing its form. What is not there gives it its use.
teachings.link: A sieve and a filter do their work with their holes. The wire only holds the holes in place. The lesson's tools separate by what they leave open.

teachings.source: A doha attributed to Kabir, the 15th-century poet of Varanasi ('Sadhu aisa chahiye, jaisa soop subhay')
teachings.teaching: Kabir says a wise person should be like a winnowing basket, which keeps the solid grain and lets the empty husk fly away.
teachings.link: Kabir uses winnowing as a picture for choosing what is worth keeping. The lesson adds a question for him: the husk that flies off feeds cattle and soil, so is anything in the basket only waste?

science.text: The atoms in your body were mixed into gas and dust between the stars before the Earth formed. Nearly all of them, except hydrogen, were made inside stars. Margaret Burbidge, with Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle, showed in 1957 how stars make them.

Can everything about a whole, such as a living cell or a mind, be explained from its separated parts? Some scientists say yes in principle. Others, following Philip Anderson, say each level has its own behaviour.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and most scientists who study the brain today
other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that only the material elements exist. Awareness, they said, appears when the elements are combined in a body, as the power to make someone drunk appears when certain ingredients ferment together. When the body comes apart, awareness ends. Most brain scientists today hold a similar view: awareness is what a working brain does. On this view matter is the ground, and there is no one essence behind it.

practice.title: One breath, sorted
practice.say: Sit comfortably and let your hands rest. Breathe in slowly through your nose. That breath is a mixture of gases. Hold it gently and count to three. Right now your lungs are taking some oxygen out of it. Breathe out slowly. What leaves has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide. A plant near you may take that in. Do this for five slow breaths. Each time, notice that you are taking a little from the mixture and giving a little back. After the fifth breath, sit still for a moment. Ask yourself: where did the air stop and where did I begin?
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe in slowly and count to three. Your lungs are taking oxygen out of the air right now. Breathe out slowly and think of a plant taking in what you gave back. Do this five times, then sit quietly and ask where the air stops and you begin.

ask: The filtered water looked pure and was not. What else around you might look like one thing only because nobody has tested it closely?
Your body takes in air, water and food and gives them back changed. Which part of that mixture would you point to and say 'this is me'?
The salt was in the sea before anyone separated it. Was it 'salt' then, or did separating make it salt?
If nothing that is separated ever leaves the world, what does 'throwing something away' mean?

playtest: Planned from the parts the cards teach and checked by reasoning, not yet tried by a family. Check first: the mud, salt and water test (e1) with a pot-soil sample, a coffee filter and a steel plate. The filtrate may be faintly tea-coloured from dissolved soil, and two tablespoons spread thin on a wide plate should leave a visible white film within 1 to 3 days. Try the same test with rava in place of soil: the filtrate is cloudy with starch and the crust is off-white, which is why the lesson uses clean sand in the hands-on version. Check that an ordinary fridge magnet picks steel pins through a thin bag (a2), that two of three washable black pens split on a coffee filter (e2), that a table fan on its lowest speed carries paper bits off a falling stream of rice (a3), and that food colour spreads visibly faster in a very warm tumbler than a cold one within 10 minutes (a4). Facts still to verify before publishing: Sushruta Samhita Sutrasthana 45 and its date, Arthashastra 2.12, Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.6 (some editions 1.1.5), Tattvartha Sutra 5.33 (5.32 in some editions), Milindapanha Book 2 chapter 1, the Charvaka reference in the Sarvadarshanasamgraha, Chandogya 6.10 and 6.13, Tao Te Ching 11, Anaxagoras fragments 6 and 11, Siddhasena Divakara's date, the Colwell study dates and the halving of cholera, Rayleigh 1892 and argon 1894, heavy hydrogen 1931, the Minjur plant, the SWaCH and Hasiru Dala details, ilmenite at Chavara and Manavalakurichi, the share of Gujarat in India's salt, and the flamingo, gypsum and bittern details at Thoothukudi in the story. Numbers to check: sea water 35 grams of salt a litre, kidneys 180 litres filtered and 1.5 litres passed, nectar more than half water and honey under one fifth, 22-carat gold as 22 parts in 24, filter paper holes about 0.01 millimetre, a bacterium about 0.001 millimetre. Parent notes: nothing in the soil tests is to be tasted. A grown-up cuts the plastic bottle in the filter challenge. Clear filtered water is not safe to drink unless it is boiled or treated.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of.
terms.example: A steel spoon is made of steel and a wooden spoon is made of wood.
terms.art: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon side by side, each labelled with its material.

terms.meaning: Two or more materials put together, each still the same material.
terms.example: Stir a cup of rice into a cup of toor dal and you have a mixture of rice and dal.
terms.art: A steel bowl holding white rice and yellow toor dal stirred together.

terms.meaning: Something a material does or has, such as its colour, its taste or being pulled by a magnet.
terms.example: Salt is white, tastes salty and disappears in water. Those are three of its properties.
terms.art: A heap of white salt with three labels: white, salty, dissolves in water.

terms.meaning: To take the parts of a mixture apart so that each part is by itself.
terms.example: Picking the stones out of a plate of rice separates the stones from the rice.
terms.art: A hand lifting a small grey stone out of a plate of rice.

terms.meaning: Taking one part out of a mixture one piece at a time, using a difference your eyes or fingers can tell.
terms.example: A grandmother spreads dal on a plate and picks out the tiny stones.
terms.art: Fingers flicking a grey stone out of yellow dal on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: A sheet or net with holes of one size. Small pieces fall through and big pieces stay on top.
terms.example: An atta sieve lets flour fall through and holds back the brown bran flakes.
terms.art: A round steel sieve with flour falling through it and brown flakes left on the mesh.

terms.meaning: Letting moving air carry the light pieces of a mixture away while the heavy pieces fall straight down.
terms.example: A farmer pours paddy from a flat basket in a breeze, and the husk blows to one side.
terms.art: A woman holding a flat basket above her head, grain falling in a heap and husk drifting sideways.

terms.meaning: The dry, light outer covering of a grain.
terms.example: Paddy has a husk around each rice grain, and the husk is removed before the rice is cooked.
terms.art: A heap of golden paddy with a handful of pale husk beside it.

terms.meaning: Leaving a mixture still so that heavier solid pieces sink to the bottom of a liquid.
terms.example: Wash rice, wait a few seconds, and the rice sinks while the dust stays in the water.
terms.art: A steel bowl of rice and cloudy water with rice grains resting at the bottom.

terms.meaning: Tipping the clear liquid from the top of a settled mixture without stirring up the bottom layer. Its other name is decanting.
terms.example: After rice settles, you pour the cloudy washing water into the sink and keep the rice.
terms.art: A bowl tilted over a sink, cloudy water flowing out and rice staying in the bowl.

terms.meaning: The pull that makes a dropped stone fall to the ground. Scientists describe it in more than one way, and no theory yet joins gravity with quantum physics.
terms.example: A dropped pin falls to the floor, and gravity also pulls sand to the bottom of a tumbler of water.
terms.art: A pin falling from a hand to the floor with a downward arrow.

terms.meaning: To spread out into a liquid as particles so small that you cannot see them.
terms.example: Salt stirred into water dissolves. The water looks clear, but it tastes salty.
terms.art: A spoon stirring white salt into a clear tumbler, with the salt grains getting smaller.

terms.meaning: A liquid with something dissolved in it.
terms.example: Salt water is a solution of salt in water, and so is sweet tea.
terms.art: A tumbler of clear water with a few tiny dots drawn inside to show dissolved salt.

terms.meaning: A material with holes too small for solid pieces to pass, used to hold the solid back and let the liquid through.
terms.example: A tea strainer is a filter that holds back the leaves and lets the tea pass.
terms.art: Tea pouring through a steel strainer into a cup, leaves staying in the strainer.

terms.meaning: How hard something pushes on each small part of a surface.
terms.example: Press a thumb on a table, then press with a fingertip. The fingertip pushes harder on each small spot.
terms.art: A thumb and a fingertip pressing on a table, with arrows of different sizes.

terms.meaning: The liquid that has come through a filter.
terms.example: The tea in the cup, after it has been strained, is the filtrate.
terms.art: A cup of clear tea below a strainer, with an arrow labelled filtrate.

terms.meaning: The solid that stays behind on a filter or at the bottom of a dish.
terms.example: The wet tea leaves left in the strainer are the residue.
terms.art: A strainer holding a small heap of wet tea leaves, with an arrow labelled residue.

terms.meaning: A liquid changing into a gas and leaving the surface. When salt water evaporates, the water leaves and the salt stays.
terms.example: Wet clothes dry on a line because their water evaporates into the air.
terms.art: A shallow plate of salt water in sunlight with wavy arrows rising from the water.

terms.meaning: A number that physicists work out and that stays the same while things change. Nobody yet knows finally what energy is, but the number works.
terms.example: The Sun gives the energy that dries a plate of salt water, and your arm gives the energy to stir.
terms.art: The Sun above a plate of salt water, with arrows going down to the plate.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. You cannot see it, and it is always in the air.
terms.example: The steam you can see above a pot is made of tiny drops. The water vapour that makes them is invisible.
terms.art: Wavy arrows rising from a wet cloth on a line into the air.

terms.meaning: To change from a gas back into a liquid, usually by cooling.
terms.example: A cold glass of water gets tiny drops on the outside when water vapour in the air condenses on it.
terms.art: A glass of ice water on a table with drops of water on the outside.

terms.meaning: To pull something closer, without needing to touch it first.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a steel pin across a small gap, before they touch.
terms.art: A magnet above a steel pin with the pin leaping up towards it.

terms.meaning: Able to be attracted by a magnet. Iron and steel are magnetic.
terms.example: A paper clip is magnetic. A plastic comb and a pencil are not.
terms.art: A magnet picking up a paper clip while a plastic comb stays on the table.

terms.meaning: The pull between magnets, and between a magnet and things such as iron.
terms.example: A fridge magnet that sticks to a steel door shows magnetism.
terms.art: A fridge magnet clinging to a steel fridge door.

terms.meaning: A piece of a material so small that you cannot see it.
terms.example: Each grain of salt holds an enormous number of particles, too small to see even with a magnifying glass.
terms.art: A grain of salt drawn very large, split into many tiny dots.

terms.meaning: A change in which materials join and become a new material that cannot simply be taken apart again.
terms.example: Lemon juice added to milk makes lumps and a thin liquid, and you cannot get smooth milk back.
terms.art: A cup of milk with lemon juice turning into white lumps and a yellow-green liquid.

terms.meaning: A way of separating a mixture by letting a liquid creep through paper, carrying each part along at its own speed.
terms.example: Water climbing a paper strip splits black ink into bands of blue, pink and yellow.
terms.art: A paper strip hanging in a tumbler of water with a black dot splitting into coloured bands.

terms.meaning: A mixture so evenly mixed that it looks the same all through. Scientists call it a homogeneous mixture.
terms.example: A glass of salt water, or the air in a room, is a uniform mixture.
terms.art: A tumbler of clear salt water beside a bowl of bhel puri.

terms.meaning: A mixture whose different parts you can see. Scientists call it a heterogeneous mixture.
terms.example: Bhel puri is a mixture of puffed rice, onion and sev, and you can see each part.
terms.art: A plate of bhel puri with the puffed rice, onion and sev picked out in colour.

terms.meaning: Made of one substance only. In everyday talk it also means clean and safe.
terms.example: A shop calls a bottle of water pure when it is clean. A chemist asks whether it holds only water.
terms.art: Two tumblers of clear water, one labelled clean and one labelled only water.

terms.meaning: How much of a sample is the named substance, written as a number such as 99.9 out of 100.
terms.example: Gold sold as 999 is 999 parts gold in every 1,000, and the other part is something else.
terms.art: A gold bar stamped 999 beside a gold bangle stamped 916.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms joined together as one piece. Water is made of molecules.
terms.example: One water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom joined together.
terms.art: A bent blue and red ball model of one water molecule.

terms.meaning: Water whose hydrogen atoms are a rare heavier kind. It is separated from ordinary water in special plants.
terms.example: India makes heavy water in plants for some of its nuclear power stations.
terms.art: Two tumblers of water, one labelled ordinary and one heavy, looking exactly alike.

terms.meaning: The physics of very small things, such as atoms and particles, which behave quite differently from everyday things.
terms.example: Quantum physics says that two particles of the same kind are exactly alike, with no hidden label.
terms.art: Two identical tiny balls with no marks on them.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how many ways the parts of a mixture can be arranged. A mixed state has far more ways than a separated one.
terms.example: There are only a few ways for all the blue ink to sit in one drop. There is a huge number of ways for it to spread through the tumbler.
terms.art: A drop of blue ink spreading through a tumbler in four stages.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece that old Indian philosophers of the Vaisheshika school said cannot be cut any further.
terms.example: In their account, a clay pot is made when paramanu come together, and it ends when they come apart.
terms.art: Tiny dots joining into a clay pot shape, then separating again.

terms.meaning: A Sanskrit word for things coming together, one of the two ideas the Vaisheshika thinkers used to explain mixing and making.
terms.example: Rice and dal poured into one bowl show samyoga. Picking them apart again shows vibhaga.
terms.art: Two hands pouring rice and dal into one bowl.

terms.meaning: A Sanskrit word for things coming apart, the partner of samyoga.
terms.example: Winnowing, where the husk leaves the grain, is vibhaga that anyone can see.
terms.art: A winnowing basket with husk drifting away from falling grain.

terms.meaning: Water with a lot of salt dissolved in it.
terms.example: Sea water is thin brine, and the water in a salt pan gets saltier day by day until it is thick brine.
terms.art: A salt pan with greyish water and a pile of white salt at its edge.

terms.meaning: A metal made by mixing two or more metals, or a metal and another material, so that it looks like one metal.
terms.example: A 22-carat gold bangle is an alloy of gold with a little copper or silver.
terms.art: A gold bangle with two small labels showing gold and copper.

warmup.q: Stir sugar into tea. Is the sugar still in the tea? How could you tell?
warmup.a: Yes. You can taste that the tea is sweet, even though you cannot see the sugar.

warmup.q: Name one thing in your kitchen that is a mixture.
warmup.a: Any real mixture, such as rice and dal in a bowl, salt water, tea, or bhel puri.

warmup.q: How do you get the stones out of a plate of rice?
warmup.a: Spread the rice and pick the stones out by hand. A sieve also works if the stones are bigger than the grains.

warmup.q: Why does a tea strainer keep the leaves but let the tea through?
warmup.a: Its holes are bigger than the tea but smaller than the leaves.

warmup.q: What happens to a plate of salt water left in the sun for two days?
warmup.a: The water goes into the air and a white crust of salt is left on the plate.

warmup.q: What does a magnet pick up from a bowl of rice and steel pins?
warmup.a: The steel pins. Iron and steel are attracted by a magnet and rice is not.

warmup.q: When you wash rice, why does the water turn cloudy?
warmup.a: Fine dust and loose starch spread in the water. The rice grains are heavy and sink.

warmup.q: Where does the water go when wet clothes dry on a line?
warmup.a: It evaporates into the air as water vapour.

quiz: Salt stirred into water has turned into water.
The salt is still there. The water tastes salty, and evaporation brings the salt back.
A magnet can pick steel pins out of a bowl of rice.
Steel is attracted by a magnet and rice is not.
A sieve separates things by their size.
Pieces smaller than the holes fall through and bigger ones stay on top.
A filter can take dissolved salt out of water.
Dissolved salt is far smaller than the holes in a filter, so it passes straight through.
Evaporation leaves the dissolved solid behind.
The water leaves as vapour and the solid cannot follow.
Winnowing uses moving air to carry away light pieces.
Husk is lighter than grain, so a breeze blows it farther.
Lemon juice and milk make a mixture you can unmix by picking.
A new material forms, so picking or sieving cannot give the milk back.
Air is a mixture of gases.
Air holds nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
Much of the rain that falls is water the Sun has lifted out of the sea, leaving the salt behind.
The Sun evaporates sea water, and the salt stays behind in the sea.
Clear water that looks clean has only water in it.
Clear water usually holds dissolved minerals and gases too.
odd: A spoon only moves things. The other three each use a difference between the parts to separate them.
Cooking makes new materials. The other three only separate.
Lemon makes a new material in milk. The other three can be taken apart again.
Evaporation, melting and condensing are changes between solid, liquid and gas. Dissolving is a solid spreading into a liquid.
Husk, chaff and bran are bits of grain plants. Salt is a mineral.

spotted.text: When you wash rice or dal, swirl it and wait a few seconds. Notice that the grains sink and the cloudy water sits on top. Pour the cloud away and see how the water clears.
spotted.art: A steel bowl of rice with cloudy water above and grains resting below, a hand tilting it over a sink.

spotted.text: Watch someone make South Indian filter coffee. Hot water drips through the powder in the metal filter, and the dark decoction comes out below. Notice that the powder stays behind.
spotted.art: A steel filter coffee set with dark decoction dripping into the lower cup and wet powder in the upper one.

spotted.text: Look at how a cook uses a flat winnowing tray, called a soop in Hindi or a muram in Tamil. She tosses dal gently and the light husk flies off while the dal falls back. Notice that she does not touch each grain.
spotted.art: A woman tossing dal in a flat bamboo tray, light husk drifting off the edge.

spotted.text: When paneer is made, milk is curdled with lemon or vinegar and then poured through a muslin cloth. Notice that the lumps stay in the cloth and the thin liquid runs through. Two different changes happen in one kitchen.
spotted.art: A muslin cloth held over a bowl with white paneer lumps inside and thin liquid dripping below.

spotted.text: After a hot day or a game, look at your school shirt or your forehead. A white salty mark can be left where sweat dried. Notice that the water left and the salt stayed.
spotted.art: A blue school shirt with a pale white salty patch under the arm.

spotted.text: Look inside a steel kettle, a water bottle or a tap. A chalky white ring or crust is left where drops of hard water evaporated. Notice that the water vanished and the minerals stayed.
spotted.art: The inside of a steel kettle with a white chalky ring at the water line.

spotted.text: In the monsoon, look at how muddy puddle water sits still for an hour. Notice that it slowly clears at the top and a thin layer of mud lies at the bottom. Nobody added a filter.
spotted.art: A clear plastic tumbler of muddy water on a windowsill, with the top half paler than the bottom.

spotted.text: Next time someone chops onion or pours out a bowl of tea, look at the tea strainer. Notice which part stays and which part goes through, and think about which difference between them the strainer uses.
spotted.art: A steel tea strainer above a cup, leaves in the strainer and tea in the cup.

applications: Salt pans at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu and in the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat use evaporation on a huge scale. Sea water or brine from underground is led through a row of shallow ponds. The Sun and wind take the water, and white salt is raked from the last pond. Gujarat gives about three quarters of the salt made in India.

Waste pickers in Indian cities sort the rubbish that other people mix. Groups such as SWaCH in Pune and Hasiru Dala in Bengaluru work with households who keep wet and dry waste apart. This makes picking faster and safer. The same picking you did with stones in rice is done here by hand, all day.

Beach sand at Chavara in Kerala and Manavalakurichi in Tamil Nadu holds dark grains of the mineral ilmenite. Strong magnets attract it, and it is used to make titanium. Factories pass the sand over magnets and heavy-grain tables to part the minerals by their differences.

Water works in cities clear river water in steps. First the water stands in large tanks so that mud settles. Then it passes through beds of sand, which are filters. Last, it is treated to kill germs, because settling and filtering do not stop the smallest germs.

A sari folded several times was used as a filter for drinking water in villages in Bangladesh. The microbiologist Rita Colwell and her team tested it, and cholera fell by about half. Cloth did not make the water pure. It held back the larger bits that carry the germs.

Rice mills use sieves to sort whole grains from broken ones. Some use machines that look at the colour of each grain and blow out the discoloured ones with a jet of air. This is picking, done by a camera and fast air instead of fingers.

In your kidneys, the filters pass about 180 litres of liquid a day from your blood, and nearly all of it goes back to the blood. About 1.5 litres leave your body as urine, carrying waste. Your body separates mixtures all day without you noticing.

Home water purifiers use cloth, ceramic or carbon filters and sometimes a thin sheet that passes water but not salt, in a process called reverse osmosis. The same ideas apply on a bigger scale at sea-water plants such as the one at Minjur near Chennai.
ask_kids: You walked to the shop today. If you took a bag of rice, which parts of the day's journey were mixtures, and could you have separated them?
Think of something you use every day that is a mixture and looks like one thing. What would you test to show it has more than one part?
If you had to get salt back from a bucket of muddy sea water, what would you do first, and why not last?
Which is easier at home, mixing two things or separating them again? What makes the difference?
A cook, a farmer and a scientist each separate something. What is the same about what they do?
When something looks clear, like water or glass, what could still be hidden inside it?
If you could never use a sieve, a filter, a magnet or the Sun again, what could you still do to clean a bowl of rice?
What is the mixture you are made of? Name three materials in your body that you could not see from outside.

maths.problem: Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in each litre. How many litres of sea water must dry up to leave 1 kilogram of salt?
maths.explain: 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. 1,000 ÷ 35 is about 28.6, which rounds up to 29 litres. A salt pan makes tonnes of salt, so it must dry up millions of litres.
maths.context: This problem uses the salt in sea water to find how much water must evaporate to make salt.
maths.why_maths: A fixed amount of salt in each litre is a ratio. Scaling the ratio up tells salt makers how big a pond they need.

maths.problem: A long thin rice grain is 6 millimetres long and 1.5 millimetres wide and thick. Three sieves have round holes of 1, 2.5 and 7 millimetres. Which sieves stop the grain, and which let it pass?
maths.answer: The 1 millimetre sieve stops it. The 2.5 and 7 millimetre sieves let it pass.
maths.explain: A grain can go through a hole if its smallest cross-section fits. The grain is 1.5 millimetres across when it goes end-first. That is smaller than 2.5, so it passes. It is bigger than 1, so it is stopped. The 7 millimetre hole is bigger than the longest side, so it passes at any angle.
maths.context: This problem asks which holes a grain fits through, which is the whole idea of sieving.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a piece with a hole is how you choose a sieve. It shows that the smallest side of a piece decides if it passes.

maths.problem: Filter paper has holes about 0.01 millimetres wide. A sand grain is about 0.5 millimetres wide. A bacterium is about 0.001 millimetres long. How many times wider is the sand grain than a hole, and how many bacteria in a line fit across one hole?
maths.answer: The sand grain is 50 times wider than a hole. About 10 bacteria fit across one hole.
maths.explain: 0.5 ÷ 0.01 = 50. 0.01 ÷ 0.001 = 10. The paper stops sand easily and lets a line of 10 bacteria through, so clear filtered water can still carry germs.
maths.context: This problem compares three very different sizes against the size of a hole in a filter.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one size by another tells you how many times bigger it is. It shows why a filter that stops sand does not stop germs.

maths.problem: A girl mixes 10 grams of sand with 10 grams of salt in water. She filters, dries the sand and gets 10 grams. She dries the filtrate and gets 9 grams of salt. Where did 1 gram go? Give two likely reasons.
maths.answer: It was not destroyed. Likely reasons are salt left stuck to the filter or wet sand, and some salt left on the tumbler or the spoon.
maths.explain: Nothing that is separated is lost. The 1 gram is somewhere in the apparatus. Rinsing the sand and the tumbler into the filtrate would bring most of it back. A total of 19 grams for 20 grams put in is a clue to look for the missing gram, not for an error in nature.
maths.context: This problem checks a separation by adding up what came back and asking where the difference went.
maths.why_maths: Adding the parts back together is how scientists check that a separation did not lose anything. The gap points to where to look.

experiments.title: The mud, salt and water test
experiments.question: Muddy salt water is filtered until it looks clear. Is there still salt in the clear water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things. Will the water look clear after filtering? Will anything be left when a spoonful dries? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Two plates are dried side by side in the same place. Plate A holds the filtered water. Plate B holds plain tap water from the same tap, in the same amount. Only the thing on the plate is different. Plate B shows how much a plain spoonful of your tap water leaves, so you do not blame the salt for what the tap water leaves.
results_table: What is left when a spoonful dries

materials.item: 2 clear plastic tumblers, each holding about 250 millilitres
2 level tablespoons of fine soil from a plant pot, with stones and twigs picked out
2 level tablespoons of table salt
1 cup of tap water, about 200 millilitres, and a little more for plain water
a coffee filter paper, or a double layer of white kitchen tissue
a steel bowl to catch the poured-off water
a steel tea strainer or a plastic funnel to hold the filter over a tumbler
a clean cotton handkerchief or cloth
2 wide steel plates or thalis, as flat as you can find
a spoon, a pencil and paper
a hand magnifying glass, or a phone camera that can zoom

experiments.safety: Do not taste the muddy water, the filtered water or the crust. Soil carries germs, and filtering does not remove all of them. Wash your hands afterwards and pour the leftover mud on a plant pot or a drain, not in the kitchen sink.

schedule.what: Mix the mud and salt, let it settle, filter it until clear and put two plates in the sun.
Look at both plates. If plate A is still wet, check it again the next day.

experiments.record: Fill in the three columns of the table for the four liquids. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this investigation you make muddy salt water and filter it until it looks clear. Then you dry a little of the clear water to find out if the salt is still there.

setup.art: Two clear tumblers on a table, one holding brown muddy water with soil swirling and one holding plain clear water.
setup.caption: 1. Stir soil and salt into one tumbler of water. Keep a tumbler of plain tap water beside it.

setup.art: A coffee filter paper folded into a cone and held in a steel tea strainer over a clear tumbler, with brown water being poured in.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the muddy water slowly through a coffee filter held in a strainer.

setup.art: A clear tumbler of filtered water next to a tumbler of plain water, both standing on a sheet of white paper.
setup.caption: 3. Put the filtered water beside plain water and look at both against white paper.

setup.art: Two steel plates on a sunny windowsill, one with a thin film of filtered water and one with plain water, labelled A and B.
setup.caption: 4. Spread two spoonfuls of each on a plate and leave both in the sun.

flow.do: Put two clear tumblers on the table. Fill the first with about one cup of tap water, which is a small steel tumbler three-quarters full. Stick a paper label on it and write A. Fill the second with the same amount of tap water and label it B. Put tumbler B to one side for later.
flow.say: Tumbler B is our plain water, so we have something to compare with. What do you think we will do with the other one?
flow.kid: Fill two tumblers with the same amount of water. Label one A and one B. Put B to one side.
flow.parent: Use the same tap for both tumblers. The plain tumbler B will later show what ordinary tap water looks like and how much it leaves on a plate.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason before mixing, and write both down. Then stir 2 level tablespoons of fine soil and 2 level tablespoons of salt into tumbler A. Stir for a full minute until the salt has gone and the water is brown. Do not taste it.
flow.say: We are making muddy salt water. After we filter it, do you think the water will be clear? Will anything of the salt come back when we dry it? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Say what you think and why. Then stir the soil and salt into tumbler A for one minute. Do not taste it.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The test will answer it. If a few salt grains stay at the bottom, stir for another minute. Two level tablespoons of salt dissolve in this much water at room temperature.

flow.do: Leave tumbler A still for 5 minutes. Look at the layers. Then pour the top liquid slowly into the steel bowl, stopping before the mud at the bottom moves. Pour the thick mud at the bottom into a pot of soil and rinse the tumbler.
flow.say: What has sunk? Is the water on top clear now? You have just done settling and pouring off.
flow.kid: Wait 5 minutes. Then pour the top liquid into a bowl and keep the mud behind.

ask.q: What do you notice about the water on top, after the mud has settled?
good: It is paler, but still cloudy.
The big bits sank and the finest bits are still floating.

flow.parent: The top liquid will still be brown and cloudy. The finest bits of soil sink slowest, which is why settling alone is not enough. Use a bowl you can rinse well afterwards.

flow.do: Fold a coffee filter into a cone and rest it in a tea strainer over a clean tumbler. Pour the cloudy water from the bowl into the cone, a little at a time. Catch the drips. If the liquid is still cloudy, pour it back through the same paper. Do this up to three times. If the paper clogs and nothing drips, use a fresh paper.
flow.say: The paper has holes too small for the mud to pass. What do you think comes through, and what stays on the paper? Look at the colour of what is dripping.
flow.kid: Pour the cloudy water slowly through the filter paper. Pour it back through again until it looks clear.

ask.q: What is left on the paper, and what came through?
good: The mud stayed on the paper.
Water, and whatever dissolved in it, came through.

flow.parent: A coffee filter drips slowly, so this takes 5 to 10 minutes. For a faster start, pour first through a clean folded handkerchief and then through the paper. If you have no strainer, fix the paper over the tumbler's mouth with a rubber band and let it sag a little. The clear liquid that comes through is the filtrate, and the mud left on the paper is the residue.

flow.do: Put the filtered water beside tumbler B on a sheet of white paper. Look at both from the side and from above. Hold them up to the window. Fill in the 'Clear or cloudy?' column for each liquid.
flow.say: Can you tell which tumbler holds the filtered water and which holds the plain water? Could we tell if there is salt in the filtered one, just by looking?
flow.kid: Put the two tumblers side by side. Look hard. Can you tell which is which?
flow.parent: Do not taste either tumbler. The filtered water may look very slightly yellow or tea-coloured. That colour is something dissolved from the soil that went through the paper, and it is a result too. If it is still cloudy, filter it one more time with fresh paper.

check.q: The filtered water looks as clear as the plain water. What does that tell you?
options: The mud pieces are held back
check.why: The paper holds back mud pieces that are bigger than its holes. Clear to the eye does not mean nothing is dissolved, because dissolved pieces are far too small to see. If you picked 'the salt has gone', see what the plates show.

flow.do: Pour 2 tablespoons of the filtered water on one steel plate. Pour 2 tablespoons of plain water from tumbler B on the other plate. Tilt each plate so the liquid spreads in a thin film. Mark the plates A and B with paper labels. Put both on a sunny windowsill or in a warm breezy spot, lying level.
flow.say: Plate A holds the filtered water. Plate B holds plain tap water. What do you think we will find on each plate when the water has gone?
flow.kid: Spread two spoonfuls of filtered water on plate A. Spread plain water on plate B. Put both in the sun.
flow.parent: Two tablespoons spread thin on a wide plate usually dry in one day in sun. On a humid, cloudy day they take two or three days. If the plates are still wet after three days, put them in front of a table fan on a low setting. Keep both plates in the same place.

flow.do: Next day, look at both plates. Look at them with a magnifying glass. Plate A should show a white crust or a ring of tiny white crystals. Plate B should show nothing, or only a faint ghost ring. Write three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why. Do not taste the crust.
flow.say: What is on plate A? What is on plate B? What does the difference tell you about the filtered water?
flow.kid: Look at both plates with a magnifying glass. Write what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: If your tap water is hard, plate B leaves a faint ring of dissolved minerals. Plate A should leave far more, because the filtered water also holds the added salt. This test cannot tell us if the crust is only salt. Some soil colour may also have dried on the plate. It also cannot tell what else is in the plain water, and plate B shows only what a spoon of it leaves.
flow.think: The filter paper found no second material in the water, and drying found one. What does that say about the word 'clear'? What else would you test?

experiments.title: The black pen test: is black one colour?
experiments.question: A black sketch pen makes one black line. Is the black ink a single colour, or does it hold other colours?
experiments.predict: Guess what will happen to the black dot when water climbs over it. Will it stay black or change? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The paper strips are the same paper, the same width and the same length. Each dot is made near the bottom, the same size and the same height above the water. Each strip is left in water until the water reaches the same line near the top. Only the pen is different.
results_table: Colours I saw, bottom to top
Did it split? Yes or no

materials.item: a white coffee filter or white kitchen tissue, cut or torn into strips about 2 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres long
a black washable water-based sketch pen
a green or brown water-based sketch pen
a black ballpoint pen, and a permanent marker if you have one
a wide-mouthed tumbler or small steel bowl that holds a pencil across the top
water, about a finger-width deep
a pencil and cellotape or paper clips to hang the strips from
old newspaper to dry the strips on

schedule.what: Make the dots, run the strips in water, read the bands and dry them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick the dried strips on a page and write a label under each.
experiments.context: In this investigation you test several pens to find out if each pen draws one colour or a mixture. Water carries the colours up a strip of paper.

setup.art: Four paper strips lying flat on a table, each with a pencil line near the bottom and a thick dot of a different pen on the line.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a pencil line 2 centimetres from the bottom of each strip. Make a thick dot of one pen on each line.

setup.art: A wide tumbler with about one finger-width of water and a pencil laid across the top, with paper strips hanging from it so that only their bottom edges touch the water.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the strips from a pencil so the bottom edges dip in the water, with the dots above the water.

setup.art: A paper strip with water climbing and a black dot spreading into bands of blue, pink and yellow, with a pencil mark showing where the water stopped.
setup.caption: 3. Take the strips out when the water is a thumb-width from the top. Look at the bands.

flow.do: Tear or cut four paper strips about 2 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres long. If you use scissors, an adult should hold them. Draw a pencil line across each strip 2 centimetres from one end. Write the name of a pen in pencil at the top of each strip.
flow.say: Each strip will test a different pen. Why do we draw the line in pencil and not in ink?
flow.kid: Make four strips. Draw a pencil line near the bottom of each. Write a pen's name at the top of each.
flow.parent: Pencil is not carried by water, but pen ink might be. The strip names are written at the top so they stay dry. The adult should cut the strips if the child cannot yet use scissors safely.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason, and write both down. Then make a thick round dot of about 5 millimetres on the pencil line of each strip, one pen to a strip. Press and go over the dot twice so it is dark. Let the dots dry for a minute.
flow.say: I will make a black dot with each pen. Do you think the black will stay black when water goes over it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say what you think and why. Then make a thick dark dot on each strip with a different pen.
flow.parent: A small thin dot gives pale, hard-to-see bands. A big dark dot gives clear bands. Use a washable sketch pen in black, and a green or brown water-based pen as a second choice. Include the ballpoint and the permanent marker if you have them, because they may not move at all.

flow.do: Pour water about one finger-width deep into the tumbler. Lay a pencil across the top. Hang the strips from the pencil with tape. The bottom edges should just touch the water, and the dots should stay above it. Check that the dots are not under the water.
flow.say: The water must touch the paper below the dot. What do you think will happen when the water reaches the dots?
flow.kid: Pour a little water in the tumbler. Hang the strips so only their bottom edges are in the water. The dots must stay dry.
flow.parent: If the dot goes under the water, the ink washes into the tumbler and nothing climbs. Start again with fresh strips. If the strips curl and touch, put them in separate tumblers.

flow.do: Wait and watch. The water moves up the paper slowly and passes through each dot. When the water is a thumb-width from the top of a strip, lift it out. Mark where the water stopped with a pencil. Lay the strips on newspaper to dry. Write the colours you see in the table, from the bottom up.
flow.say: What is the water doing to the black dot? Do all the dots do the same thing? What is happening to the colours?
flow.kid: Watch the water move up the paper. Take each strip out when the water is a thumb-width from the top. Write the colours you see.

ask.q: What did the black pen do, and did the other pens do the same?
good: Some black pens split into several colours.
The ballpoint and permanent marker stayed where they were.

flow.parent: On a coffee filter the water climbs about 8 to 10 centimetres in 10 minutes. Many washable black pens split into blue, purple, pink or yellow bands. Some black pens stay one dark band, and that is a result too. If your black does not split, try the green or brown pen, which nearly always does.

flow.do: Dry the strips and look at them. Write which pens split and which did not. Stick the strips onto a page. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why. Add one sentence on what this test cannot tell you.
flow.say: Which pens held more than one colour? Why would some ink travel higher than other ink in the same water?
flow.kid: Compare your strips. Which pens split and which did not? Write what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: The test shows that some inks are mixtures of colours. The colours climb at different speeds because they cling to the paper in different amounts. A band that did not split could still hold more than one thing. A different liquid, such as rubbing alcohol, might split it. That links to the idea that a test can only find what it can catch.
flow.think: If a pen stayed one band in water, could you be sure it holds only one colour? What else would you try?

experiments.title: Sand, soil and salt in water: which one leaves first?
experiments.question: Sand, soil and salt are each stirred into water. Which one leaves the water clear first, and which never leaves?
experiments.predict: Guess the order in which the three tumblers will clear. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The three tumblers hold the same amount of water, the same level tablespoon of each solid and are stirred the same number of times. They are left in the same place. Only the solid is different. The test looks at the same times for all three tumblers.

materials.item: clear plastic tumblers, each holding about 250 millilitres
water, about 200 millilitres for each tumbler
1 level tablespoon of clean fine sand, washed in a bowl first
1 level tablespoon of fine soil from a plant pot
1 level tablespoon of table salt
a spoon for each tumbler, or one spoon rinsed in between
a clock or phone timer
a sheet of white paper to stand the tumblers on
a pencil and paper for the table

schedule.what: Stir the three solids into water, then look at fixed times up to 15 minutes.
Look at the tumblers next morning and pour off the top of the soil tumbler.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for each time. Draw the three tumblers as they look next morning.
experiments.context: In this investigation you stir sand, soil and salt into three tumblers of water. You watch how fast each leaves the water, to find out how different solids behave in a liquid.

setup.art: Three clear tumblers of water in a row on white paper, labelled sand, soil and salt, with a level tablespoon of each solid beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the same amount of water in three tumblers. Label them sand, soil and salt.

setup.art: A hand stirring a tumbler with a spoon while the clock on a phone shows 0:00 beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stir each tumbler ten times, then start the timer.

setup.art: The three tumblers after some time: sand settled clearly at the bottom, soil cloudy with a brown layer, salt clear with nothing at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the tumblers at fixed times and write what you see.

flow.do: Set three clear tumblers in a row on white paper. Pour about 200 millilitres of tap water into each. Label them sand, soil and salt. Wash the sand in a bowl first. Swirl it with water and pour off the cloudy water twice, so that it holds less dust.
flow.say: We will put three different solids in three tumblers of the same water. What do you think we will see in each one?
flow.kid: Fill three tumblers with the same amount of water. Label them sand, soil and salt.
flow.parent: Washing the sand removes most of its dust, so the test shows the sand itself. Use the same tap and the same amount of water in each tumbler.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason, and write both down. Ask which tumbler will clear first, which will clear last and which will never settle. Do not correct the guess.
flow.say: Which tumbler will clear first? Which will take the longest? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Say which tumbler will clear first and which will last. Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Write the guess in a corner of the page, so the child can look back at it later.

flow.do: Put 1 level tablespoon of each solid into its own tumbler. Stir each tumbler 10 times with a clean spoon. Start the timer as soon as you put the spoon down.
flow.say: Stir the same number of times each time. Why do we stir each one the same number of times?
flow.kid: Add a spoonful to each tumbler. Stir ten times. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Rinse the spoon between tumblers, or use three spoons. One tablespoon of salt dissolves fully in 200 millilitres of water, and the salt tumbler should be clear in under a minute.

flow.do: Look at the tumblers after 30 seconds, 5 minutes and 15 minutes, and write what you see each time. Look from the side, against the white paper. Note the layers, the cloudiness and anything on the bottom. Look at the salt tumbler closely.
flow.say: Which tumbler clears first? What is in the bottom of each one? Is the salt tumbler clear because the salt has gone?
flow.kid: Look at the tumblers at 30 seconds, 5 minutes and 15 minutes. Write what you see each time.

ask.q: Why does the salt tumbler look clear, if the salt is still there?
good: The salt has dissolved into pieces too small to see.
The salt is still in the water, and you could taste it.

flow.parent: The sand usually sinks in under a minute and leaves clear water. Some fine dust may take a few minutes. The soil tumbler is still cloudy at 15 minutes, because the finest bits sink very slowly. The salt tumbler looks clear within a minute, and it is clear because the salt is dissolved. Do not taste the sand or soil tumblers. Tasting the salt tumbler is fine if you used clean drinking water and a clean tumbler.

flow.do: The next morning, look at the tumblers again. Draw the three of them. Pour the top of the soil tumbler slowly into a bowl, leaving the mud behind. Write three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why. Add one sentence on how sinking speed and dissolving differ.
flow.say: Is the soil tumbler clear now? What would you do to get the soil out faster? Which of the three could a filter help with, and which could it not?
flow.kid: Look at the tumblers. Draw what you see. Pour off the top of the soil tumbler.
flow.parent: The soil water may be clearer at the top but still slightly cloudy. Clay bits are among the smallest and sink slowest. The sand will be a clean layer, and the salt water stays clear. This test cannot tell us how long the soil takes to clear completely. A filter holds back sand and soil, and cannot take out the dissolved salt.
flow.think: Sand sinks quickly, soil sinks slowly and salt does not sink at all. What does this tell you about the pieces of each?

activities.title: Can we unmix it? Four mixtures tested
activities.context: This activity tests four mixtures to find out which can be taken apart by simple methods and which have made a new material.

materials.item: a plate with a spoon of clean fine sand and a spoon of salt
clear plastic tumblers
a clean cloth or a coffee filter
half a cup of milk at room temperature
2 tablespoons of lemon juice or vinegar
1 teaspoon of baking soda and 3 tablespoons of vinegar
a hand magnifying glass
a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Test four mixtures, then sort them by whether you could get the parts back.

activities.record: Draw a table with four rows. For each mixture write what you did, whether you could get the parts back, and how.

setup.art: A steel plate holding white salt and pale sand mixed together, with a hand lens above it.
setup.caption: 1. Mix a spoon of clean sand with a spoon of salt. Look closely and try to pick the salt out.

setup.art: Four tumblers in a row, each holding a different mixture: sand and water, salt water, milk with lemon, and fizzing baking soda with vinegar.
setup.caption: 2. Make four mixtures and ask the same question about each one.

flow.do: Mix one spoon of clean fine sand with one spoon of salt on the plate. Use sand, not rava, because rava swells and sheds starch in water. Look at the mix with a magnifying glass. Try to pick the salt out with a toothpick. Do not taste it.
flow.say: Mix 1 is sand and salt. Can you pick out the salt? How could you tell which is which?
flow.kid: Mix sand and salt on a plate. Try to pick the salt out with a toothpick.
flow.parent: Salt grains and sand grains are close in size, so fingers and eyes cannot separate them. This is the puzzle from the start of the lesson, with sand in place of rava. The mixing and the separating at the end are done in the mud, salt and water test.

flow.do: Mix 2 is sand and water. Stir a spoon of sand into a tumbler of water. Wait one minute, then pour the water through a cloth held over another tumbler. Look at what stays on the cloth and what comes through.
flow.say: Where did the sand go? Is the water clear? Can you get the sand back?
flow.kid: Stir sand into water and wait a minute. Pour it through a cloth. Look at what stays on the cloth.
flow.parent: The sand is a solid that has not dissolved, so it can be settled out and held back by a cloth. The cloth stops the sand and lets the water through.

flow.do: Mix 3 is milk and lemon. Pour half a cup of milk into a tumbler. Stir in 2 tablespoons of lemon juice or vinegar. Wait 10 minutes. If nothing has happened, stand the tumbler in a bowl of very warm tap water. Then try to get the milk back by pouring the liquid through a cloth.
flow.say: What has happened to the milk? Can you get smooth milk back again, however you try?
flow.kid: Stir lemon juice into milk. Wait and watch. Can you get smooth milk back?
flow.parent: Warm tap water helps the milk curdle faster, and you do not need a stove. The lumps and the thin liquid can be separated by the cloth, but the smooth milk never comes back. A new material formed, and the lumps are not the same as the milk was. This is how paneer is made.

flow.do: Mix 4 is baking soda and vinegar. Put 1 teaspoon of baking soda in a big tumbler. Pour in 3 tablespoons of vinegar slowly. Watch the bubbles. Wait until the fizzing stops. Try to get the baking soda back.
flow.say: What do you see? Can you get the baking soda back as it was?
flow.kid: Put baking soda in a big tumbler. Pour in vinegar. Watch what happens.
flow.parent: A new gas, carbon dioxide, forms and bubbles away, so the baking soda cannot come back as baking soda. A big tumbler stops the fizz from running over. Pour it down the drain when it stops.

flow.do: Look at your table. Sort the four mixtures into two heaps. In one heap are mixtures whose parts you could get back as they were. In the other are mixtures where a new material was made. Then ask the child the question.
flow.say: Which mixtures could you take apart again? Which ones made something new? How could you tell the difference?
flow.kid: Sort your four tests into two heaps. Say how you decided.
flow.parent: Sand and water, and sand and salt, are mixtures that keep each part. Milk with lemon and baking soda with vinegar are new materials. The test to use is: can I get each thing back just by picking, sieving, filtering or letting the water leave?
flow.think: A new material is not a mixture any more. What would you look for to tell the difference between a mixture and a new material?

activities.title: The magnet in the bag: which things does it pick?
activities.context: This activity uses a magnet to take steel pins out of rice. Then it tests everyday things with the magnet to find which are pulled.

materials.item: a steel bowl or plate
2 cups of rice
10 steel pins or paper clips
a magnet
a small plastic bag
a plate to drop the pins onto
8 small things from around the house, such as a spoon, a coin, a key, a pencil and aluminium foil

schedule.what: Take pins out of rice with a magnet in a bag, then test eight things.

activities.record: Make a table with one row for each of the eight things. Write your guess, then what the magnet did.

setup.art: A bowl of rice with silver pins hidden in it and a magnet inside a plastic bag held above the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Mix steel pins into rice. Put the magnet inside a small plastic bag.

setup.art: The bagged magnet lifted out of the rice with steel pins clinging to the bag, held over an empty plate.
setup.caption: 2. Pass the bag through the rice. Lift it out and pull the magnet from the bag so the pins drop.

setup.art: A row of eight household things, each with a tick or a cross beside it for whether the magnet picked it up.
setup.caption: 3. Test eight everyday things and mark the ones the magnet picks.

flow.do: Pour about two cups of rice into the bowl. Push 10 steel pins or paper clips in at different depths. Put the magnet inside the plastic bag. Check the magnet first by holding it over a few loose pins on the table.
flow.say: Here are ten steel pins hidden in the rice. How could we get them out without touching them?
flow.kid: Hide the pins in the rice. Put the magnet in the bag.
flow.parent: A magnet from a fridge is enough for pins and clips if the bag is thin. If nothing clings, try a stronger magnet, such as one from an old toy. The bag stops the pins from sticking to the magnet so you can drop them.

flow.do: Pass the bag slowly through the rice, close to the bottom. Lift it out and see how many pins cling to the bag. Hold it over the empty plate. Pull the magnet out of the bag, and the pins drop. Count them and add the count to your page. Repeat until the rice is clear.
flow.say: How many pins did you get on the first pass? Is there a pin left in the rice? Why does the rice stay behind?
flow.kid: Pass the bag through the rice. Lift it out. Pull out the magnet to drop the pins. Count them.
flow.parent: The rice is not magnetic, so it is not pulled. Steel is magnetic, so it clings. If the pins are deep, tilt the bowl to bring them nearer the top. Two or three passes usually take out all ten.

flow.do: Collect eight small things. Use a spoon, a key, a coin, a pencil, foil, a cloth, a plastic comb and a steel katori. Guess for each one if the magnet will pick it, and write your guess. Then test each one with the magnet, without the bag, and mark yes or no.
flow.say: Which of these will the magnet pick? Guess first and write it down. Then test each one. Did anything surprise you?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing if the magnet will pick it. Then test it.
flow.parent: Results vary between homes. A steel spoon may not be attracted, because some kinds of stainless steel are not magnetic. Some coins are and some are not. Record what your own things do, and do not correct the guess before the test.

flow.do: Look at the table. Sort the things into pulled and not pulled. Find out what the pulled things have in common. Ask the child the question.
flow.say: What do the pulled things have in common? Why can a magnet separate pins from rice and not rice from dal?
flow.kid: Sort your things into pulled and not pulled. Say what the pulled ones have in common.
flow.parent: Iron and steel are magnetic. A magnet can separate only the magnetic part, and it cannot separate two materials that are both not magnetic. Not all steel behaves the same, which is itself a fact worth noting.
flow.think: Why does a magnet only separate some mixtures? What difference between the parts must there be?

activities.title: Sieve, winnow and pour: which tool for which mess?
activities.context: This activity tries a sieve, a breeze and water on three messy mixtures. Then it uses the wrong tool on purpose, to see why the right one matters.

materials.item: 1 cup of rice with a handful of torn paper bits about the size of a grain
1 cup of atta mixed with a tablespoon of chana
a steel colander with holes of about 3 to 5 millimetres
a flour sieve with fine holes
a table fan on its lowest setting, or a window with a breeze
a large tray or sheet to catch what falls
a bowl of water
a plate and a spoon

schedule.what: Winnow the paper bits from rice, sieve the chana from atta, wash rice and pour off, then try the wrong tool.

activities.record: Draw a table with the three mixtures. Write the tool you used, the difference it used and how well it worked.

setup.art: A child pouring a thin stream of rice and paper bits from a steel plate held at shoulder height in front of a small table fan, with rice falling straight down and paper bits blown to one side.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the rice and paper bits from shoulder height in front of a gentle fan.

setup.art: A flour sieve held over a bowl with fine flour falling and a few chana beans left on the mesh.
setup.caption: 2. Shake the atta and chana through a sieve.

setup.art: A steel bowl of rice with cloudy water above it being poured gently into another bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Swirl the rice in water, let it settle, and pour off the cloudy water.

flow.do: Spread a large tray or sheet on the floor. Mix 1 cup of rice with a handful of small paper bits on a plate. Put a table fan on its lowest speed on a chair beside the tray, or stand at a window with a breeze. Check that the fan is steady.
flow.say: The paper bits are like husk in paddy. They are lighter than rice. What do you think the moving air will do to each one?
flow.kid: Mix rice and paper bits on a plate. Set up the fan beside the tray.
flow.parent: If rice blows out of the plate, turn the fan lower or stand farther away. If the paper hardly moves, stand closer. A gentle steady breeze is all you need.

flow.do: Hold the plate at shoulder height beside the fan. Tip the mixture slowly in a thin stream so that it falls past the fan onto the tray. Look at where the rice falls and where the paper bits land. Do it again with what is left, until there is no paper in the rice.
flow.say: Which falls straight down, and which blows away? Why would a farmer use this at harvest?
flow.kid: Pour the mixture slowly past the fan. Look at where the rice and the paper land.
flow.parent: This is winnowing. Light pieces are carried farther by moving air than heavy ones, so the husk-like paper lands farther away. Two or three pours usually clear the paper. Keep the rice for the next steps.

flow.do: Mix 1 cup of atta with a spoonful of chana. Pour a little at a time into the flour sieve held over a bowl and shake. Look at what falls through and what stays on the mesh. Repeat until the mesh holds only chana. Then pour the rice from the winnowing into the colander over a bowl, and note what falls through.
flow.say: What stays on the sieve? What falls through? What decides which pieces stay?
flow.kid: Shake the atta and chana in the sieve. See what stays and what falls through.
flow.parent: A sieve separates pieces by size. Atta is finer than the holes and falls through, and chana is bigger and stays. The rice grains are about 2 millimetres wide, so they fall through a colander's holes of 3 to 5 millimetres.

flow.do: Put the rice in a bowl and cover it with water. Swirl it for 10 seconds and wait 10 seconds. Look at the water. Pour the cloudy top slowly into another bowl, keeping the rice back. Look at the water that you poured away and at the rice.
flow.say: The water is cloudy. What do you think is in it? Why does the rice stay in the bowl?
flow.kid: Swirl the rice in water and wait. Pour off the cloudy top and keep the rice.
flow.parent: Dust and loose starch are fine and light, so they stay in the water, and the rice sinks. This is settling and pouring off. Use the same rice that came out of the colander.

flow.do: Now use the wrong tool on purpose. Try to separate atta from chana with the colander. Then try to separate paper bits from rice by pouring water through a sieve. Look at what happens. Write on the table which tool worked and which did not, and name the difference each tool uses.
flow.say: What happened when you used the wrong tool? What is different about the pieces that the right tool uses?
flow.kid: Try the colander on atta and chana. Say why it did not work.
flow.parent: The colander's holes are far bigger than the atta pieces, so everything falls through and nothing is separated. A tool works only if it uses a difference the parts really have.
flow.think: Every tool uses one difference. What would you do for two things with no difference at all, such as two grains of the same size, colour and weight?

activities.title: A drop of colour in still water: mixing by itself
activities.context: This activity watches a drop of food colour spread through still warm and cold water without stirring. Then it asks if the colour can be gathered back.

materials.item: clear plastic tumblers
cold tap water, about 200 millilitres
very warm tap water, about 200 millilitres, as warm as a hot bath
food colour or ink, 2 drops
a spoon
a clock or phone timer
a sheet of white paper to stand the tumblers on

schedule.what: Drop colour into cold and warm water without stirring, watch for 15 minutes, then try to gather the colour back.

activities.record: Draw the cold and the warm tumbler at 2 minutes, 6 minutes and 15 minutes. Write which spread faster.

setup.art: Two clear tumblers on white paper, one labelled cold and one labelled warm, each with one drop of blue colour sinking from the top.
setup.caption: 1. Put a drop of colour in each tumbler of still water. Do not stir.

setup.art: The two tumblers after some minutes, the warm one nearly pale blue all through and the cold one still with a dark blue patch at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Watch and draw each tumbler at the same times.

flow.do: Put two clear tumblers on a sheet of white paper. Fill one with cold tap water. Fill the other with very warm tap water from the hot tap, as warm as a hot bath, never boiling. Leave both for one minute so that the water is still. Do not touch the table again.
flow.say: We will put a drop of colour in each tumbler and not stir. Do you think the colour will spread through the whole tumbler by itself? Which tumbler will spread faster, and why?
flow.kid: Fill one tumbler with cold water and one with very warm water. Let them stand still for a minute.
flow.parent: Use the hot tap, not a kettle, so that no step is dangerous. Water warmer than a hot bath is too hot for a child to handle. Any movement of the table stirs the water, so leave it alone.

flow.do: Gently put one drop of colour on the surface in the middle of each tumbler. Do one straight after the other, and start the timer. Do not stir. Look at each tumbler from the side.
flow.say: What does the colour do when it first goes in? What do you think it will do over the next minutes?
flow.kid: Put one drop of colour into each tumbler. Do not stir. Start the timer.
flow.parent: The colour will first sink in a streak, and then spread slowly. Fast spreading in the warm tumbler is usual. If your two tumblers look about the same, do the test again, because a small difference is easy to miss.

flow.do: Look at the tumblers at 2 minutes, 6 minutes and 15 minutes. At each time, draw what you see. Write which spread farther and which looks most evenly coloured. Come back after an hour and look at both again.
flow.say: Is the colour reaching every part of the water, even though nobody stirred? What is moving it?
flow.kid: Look at the tumblers at 2, 6 and 15 minutes. Draw what you see each time.

ask.q: Why does the warm tumbler spread faster?
good: Heat makes the tiny pieces move faster.
Faster pieces bump into each other and spread out more quickly.

flow.parent: The tiny pieces of water and colour never stop moving, and they bump into one another. That spreads the colour through the whole tumbler. Warm water has faster pieces, so it spreads faster. After an hour both tumblers should be pale and even all through.

flow.do: Ask the child to try to gather the colour back into a drop with a spoon. Try for one minute. Then ask what it would take to get all the colour out of the water.
flow.say: Can you get the drop back? What would we have to do to separate the colour from the water?
flow.kid: Try to get the colour back with a spoon. Can you? What would it take?
flow.parent: The colour mixed by itself, but it cannot be gathered back by waiting. Taking it out needs work, such as filtering through charcoal or evaporating the water. Pour both tumblers down the drain when you finish.
flow.think: Mixing happens by itself, but unmixing never does. Where do you think that one-way direction comes from?

activities.title: Catch the water out of your breath
activities.context: This activity cools a steel plate and breathes on it to catch water out of your breath. Then it watches the water go back into the air.

materials.item: a steel plate or the flat lid of a steel box
a fridge or freezer
a steel tumbler of cold water with ice
a dry cloth
a clock or phone timer

schedule.what: Chill a plate, breathe on it, watch the fog clear, then look at a cold tumbler of ice water.

activities.record: Draw the plate before and after you breathe on it. Write how long the fog took to clear.

setup.art: A steel plate on a shelf inside an open fridge beside a steel tumbler of ice water.
setup.caption: 1. Chill a steel plate in the fridge for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A child breathing slowly on a cold steel plate, with a patch of fog on the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Breathe slowly onto the cold plate and watch what appears.

flow.do: Put a clean, dry steel plate in the fridge or the freezer compartment for 10 minutes. While you wait, put some ice in a steel tumbler of cold water and leave it on the table. Write down what you think will happen when you breathe on the cold plate.
flow.say: Your breath is a mixture of gases. It holds water vapour that you cannot see. What do you think will happen when it meets the cold plate?
flow.kid: Put the plate in the fridge. Put ice in a tumbler of water. Say what you think will happen.
flow.parent: Water vapour is always in the air we breathe out. A cold plate cools the vapour so that it turns back into tiny drops of water, which is called condensing.

flow.do: Take the cold plate out and hold it close to your mouth. Breathe on it slowly, as if you were fogging a mirror. Look at the plate. Do it three times in different spots. Look at the cold tumbler and see if drops have formed on the outside.
flow.say: What do you see on the plate? Where did the water come from? What happened to the tumbler?
flow.kid: Breathe slowly on the cold plate. Look at what appears. Look at the cold tumbler.
flow.parent: A grey fog of tiny drops forms on the plate, since your breath holds more water vapour than cold air can keep. On a humid day, drops also form on the outside of the cold tumbler. In dry winter air the tumbler may show less, but the plate still fogs.

flow.do: Watch the fog on the plate. Start the timer. Note how many seconds it takes to disappear. Then wipe the plate dry and breathe on it once more to check.
flow.say: Where does the fog go? How is that like wet clothes on a line?
flow.kid: Watch the fog and count the seconds until it clears. Where does it go?
flow.parent: As the plate warms in the room air, the drops evaporate back into the air as water vapour. The water you caught came out of the air and went back into it. Rain, clouds and dew follow the same path on a larger scale.

flow.do: Ask the child the question. Then ask where else in the day water is caught out of the air. Dew on a leaf and drops on a cold glass are two examples.
flow.say: You separated water from a mixture of gases, using only cold. What was the difference that cold used?
flow.kid: Think of where else water comes out of the air. Say what you notice.
flow.parent: Water vapour changes into liquid at a higher temperature than nitrogen or oxygen do. So a cold surface catches the water and leaves the other gases in the air.
flow.think: Fog on a plate, dew on a leaf and rain from a cloud all catch water out of air. What do they have in common?

projects.title: A salt pan on your windowsill: how fast does the sea dry?
projects.context: In this project you make sea water and set it out in a sunny place and a shady place. For six days you measure how fast the water leaves and when the salt appears.

materials.item: 2 wide steel plates or thalis with a rim about 1.5 centimetres high
1 litre of tap water in a jug
6 level teaspoons of table salt
a thin wooden skewer or a strip of stiff paper to measure depth
a ruler with millimetres
a hand magnifying glass
a sunny windowsill or terrace corner, and a shady spot in the same room
a pencil and graph paper

schedule.what: Make the sea water, pour 400 millilitres onto each plate and measure the depth.
Measure the depth on both plates at the same time of day.
Measure the depth on both plates again.
Measure the depth on both plates again.
Measure the depth on both plates, and look for the first crystals.
Measure for the last time, look at the crystals with a magnifying glass and draw the graph.

projects.record: Keep a table with one row for each day and two columns, sun and shade, for the depth in millimetres. Draw a line graph of depth against day, with both lines on one graph. Write what the crystals look like.

setup.art: Two wide steel plates each holding a shallow layer of water, one on a sunny windowsill and one on a shelf in the shade of the same room.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same amount of salt water onto two plates. Put one in the sun and one in the shade.

setup.art: A thin skewer dipped into the water on a plate and lifted out, showing a wet mark with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Every day, dip a skewer to the bottom and measure the wet mark.

setup.art: A plate with a few millimetres of water left and a ring of white crystals around the edge, with a hand lens above it.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the crystals through a magnifying glass when the water is almost gone.

flow.do: Stir 6 level teaspoons of salt into 1 litre of tap water until it has gone. This is about as salty as sea water. Pour 400 millilitres onto each plate. Put one plate on a sunny windowsill and the other in the shade in the same room, both lying level. Dip a skewer to the bottom of each plate, wait one second, lift it out and measure the wet mark in millimetres. Write both depths as Day 1.
flow.say: We have made sea water. Both plates hold the same water. Which plate do you think will dry first? Will the salt dry first, or the water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stir salt into water to make sea water. Pour the same amount onto two plates. Put one in the sun and one in the shade. Measure the depth.
flow.parent: Six level teaspoons in a litre is about 35 grams, which is close to real sea water. Measure at the same spot on the plate each day. A plate with a rim about 1.5 centimetres high holds 400 millilitres without spilling.

flow.do: At the same time of day, measure the depth on both plates and write it in the table. Look at the colour of the water. Is it the same as yesterday? Is the shady plate losing water too?
flow.say: How much did the water drop on each plate in one day? Is the water leaving at the same rate every day?
flow.kid: Measure both plates and write the numbers. Look at the water.
flow.parent: Most families see a drop of 2 to 6 millimetres a day in the sun and less in the shade. A cloudy or humid day slows both, which is why the shade is the fair comparison, not a clock. If the water is still deep after six days, keep going.

flow.do: Measure both plates and write the numbers. Work out how many millimetres each plate lost since the last day. Put the numbers on your graph.
flow.say: Is the plate in the sun losing water faster than the one in the shade? What do you think leaves the water, and what stays?
flow.kid: Measure both plates and write the numbers. Add them to the graph.
flow.parent: The water leaves as water vapour, and the salt stays. The salty water that remains is saltier each day.

flow.do: Measure both plates and write the numbers. Update the graph. Ask the child to guess when each plate will be dry.
flow.say: Using your graph, how many more days until each plate is dry? What would help the shady plate dry faster?
flow.kid: Measure both plates. Use your graph to guess the day each plate will be dry.
flow.parent: A straight line on the graph means the water is leaving at a steady rate. If a rainy day flattens the line, that is a result too.
