flow.do: Measure both plates. Look at the edges for the first white crystals. Look at them with the magnifying glass and draw one crystal. Do not stir or move the plates.
flow.say: Where do the crystals appear first? Why do you think the edges are the first place the water gets too salty to hold all the salt?
flow.kid: Measure both plates. Look for the first crystals at the edges. Look at them with the magnifying glass.
flow.parent: The water at the thin edges is gone first, so the salt there is left first. The crystals are tiny white cubes, which you can see under a magnifying glass. Salt crystals in a real pan grow the same way.

flow.do: Measure both plates for the last time. Look at the crust on each plate with the magnifying glass. Draw the graph in full. Write three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why. If you want, taste one crystal from the sun plate, only if the plate was clean.
flow.say: How much longer did the shady plate take? What shape are the crystals? Where did the water go?
flow.kid: Look at the crystals through the lens. Finish the graph. Write what you thought, saw and why.
flow.parent: This project cannot tell us how much of the crust is salt and how much is dissolved minerals from the tap water. Real salt pans lead the water through a series of ponds. A chalky mineral called gypsum comes out before the salt does. A bitter liquid called bittern is left at the end.
flow.think: The Sun takes the water and leaves the salt. Who owns the salt in a salt pan, the people who rake it, the land or the sea? What would you say?

projects.title: A week of keeping waste apart
projects.context: In this project your family keeps wet waste, dry waste and reusable items in separate containers for a week. You count what goes into each and ask who does the work when waste is mixed.

materials.item: 3 containers or boxes with lids
paper labels and a pen
a notebook for tally marks
old newspaper to line the containers

projects.safety: Do not put glass, sharp items, medicines, batteries or anything that was in a toilet into the boxes. An adult handles wet waste and washes hands afterwards. Empty the wet waste box every day, because it smells and attracts flies.

schedule.what: Set up three labelled containers: wet waste, dry waste and 'keep for reuse'.
Add a tally mark for each item. Notice the hardest items to place.
Add tally marks. Ask what you could reuse.
Add tally marks. Notice what you did without thinking.
Add tally marks. Notice what the family says.
Add tally marks. Check that each box holds only its own kind.
Count each tally, draw a bar chart and talk about who would do the sorting if the waste were mixed.

projects.record: Keep a tally chart with one row for each day and one column for each box. On day 7 draw a bar chart of the totals and write one sentence about the hardest item to place.

setup.art: Three boxes in a row with labels reading wet waste, dry waste and keep for reuse, each with a different kind of item drawn on top.
setup.caption: 1. Label three boxes and put them near the kitchen.

setup.art: A page with a tally chart of three columns and seven rows, marks in each cell.
setup.caption: 2. Add a tally mark each time something goes into a box.

flow.do: Set up three boxes near the kitchen. Label them 'wet waste', 'dry waste' and 'keep for reuse'. Put a sheet of newspaper at the bottom of each. Draw a tally chart in the notebook. Explain what goes where. Peels, leftovers and used tea leaves go in wet. Paper, plastic and metal go in dry. Jars and boxes that can be used again go in reuse.
flow.say: Rubbish is a mixture. When it is mixed, someone has to take it apart. Who do you think does that, and how? For a week we will keep it apart from the start.
flow.kid: Label three boxes: wet waste, dry waste and keep for reuse. Draw a tally chart.
flow.parent: Many Indian cities already ask families to keep wet and dry waste apart. If yours does, use the same boxes. Do not put in sharp things or glass. An adult should handle the wet waste.

flow.do: Each time something goes into a box, add a tally mark in the notebook. Look out for things that are hard to place, such as a tea bag or a milk packet. Write them in the notebook.
flow.say: Which box does this go in? Why? Is there something you are not sure about?
flow.kid: Put each thing in a box and add a tally mark. Note anything hard to place.
flow.parent: Wash milk packets before they go into dry waste, so they are clean. A tea bag holds a plastic part in many brands, so a bag may be wet and dry together. That is a good example of a mixture that is hard to separate.

flow.do: Add tally marks. Look in the reuse box. Ask what could be used again, such as a jar for a plant or a box for storing, and use one thing.
flow.say: What did you keep for reuse today? How is reusing different from throwing away or from separating?
flow.kid: Add tally marks. Pick one thing from the reuse box and find a new use for it.
flow.parent: Reusing keeps a material from becoming rubbish at all. It is the one step with no sorting.

flow.do: Add tally marks. Notice what you now do without thinking. Ask each person at home to put at least one item into the right box without being told.
flow.say: Is it getting easier? Who in the house was the first to learn which box is which?
flow.kid: Add tally marks. Notice what is getting easier.
flow.parent: A habit forms in about a week for something this small. Notice whose job the sorting becomes, and whether it is shared fairly.

flow.do: Add tally marks. Ask one person who does not live with you how waste is handled where they live. A neighbour or a relative on the phone will do. Write what they say.
flow.say: What do other homes do with their waste? Who takes it away? What happens to it next?
flow.kid: Add tally marks. Ask someone outside your home how they handle waste.
flow.parent: In many places, waste pickers walk the streets collecting and sorting. Their work is hard, and it is often poorly paid. A neat box at home makes that work easier.

flow.do: Add tally marks. Check each box to see that it holds only its own kind. Move anything in the wrong box.
flow.say: Is each box clean of the wrong things? What was the commonest mistake?
flow.kid: Check each box. Move anything that is in the wrong place.
flow.parent: If a box is mixed, the sorting has to be done later by someone else. Checking now is the same as picking.

flow.do: Count the tally marks in each column. Draw a bar chart of the totals. Write one sentence on the item that was hardest to place. Talk about the questions. Empty the boxes as your area asks.
flow.say: Which box had the most? What would happen to a mixed bin? Who would have to sort it, and who should be paid for it?
flow.kid: Count the tallies. Draw a bar chart. Write one sentence on the hardest item.
flow.parent: This project cannot show us what happens to the waste after it leaves your home. In most cities that depends on the system. Waste pickers are usually the ones who do the final separating. Some groups, such as SWaCH in Pune and Hasiru Dala in Bengaluru, are organised so that waste pickers are paid and respected.
flow.think: Is it fairer to mix waste and pay someone to sort it later, or to keep it apart from the start? Who does the work, and who gets the benefit, in each case?

challenges.title: Four things in one bowl: plan the steps and get them all back
challenges.context: This is a design problem. A bowl holds steel pins, chana, clean sand and salt. You plan the steps that get all four back, each by itself, and then try the plan.
challenges.problem: Steel pins, chana, clean fine sand and salt are mixed in a dry bowl. Plan and carry out a way to get each one back on its own plate, with as few steps as you can. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you have at home. Do not taste anything.
Every part must be returned, and the salt must come back as dry salt, which takes a day on a plate in the sun.
Write the plan before you start, and say which difference each step uses.
Try the plan once, and then change one step to see if it gets better.
materials: a bowl with 1 spoon each of pins, chana, sand and salt
a magnet, a colander or sieve, and a spoon
a tumbler of water and a coffee filter or clean cloth
four plates and a steel plate for drying the salt

setup.art: A bowl holding steel pins, chana beans, pale sand and white salt, with four empty plates beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the four parts in a bowl and put four empty plates beside it.

setup.art: A plan on paper with boxes and arrows, each box naming a method and the difference it uses.
setup.caption: 2. Plan the steps as boxes and arrows before you start.

flow.do: Write each of the four parts on paper, and next to each, write one way it is different from the other three. Use words like size, being pulled by a magnet and dissolving. Do not start yet.
flow.say: Four things are in the bowl. For each, what is it that the other three do not do?
flow.kid: List the four parts. For each one, write one difference from the others.

ask.q: What difference does each part have?
good: Steel is attracted by a magnet.
Chana is much bigger than sand and salt.
Salt dissolves in water and sand does not.

flow.parent: Steel is the only magnetic one. Chana is the biggest. Salt is the only one that dissolves. Sand is the one left over, which is also a difference.

flow.do: Plan the steps on paper. Write each step as a box, with the method and the difference it uses. Arrange the boxes in an order. Compare your plan with another person's if there is one.
flow.say: Which step comes first? Why does the order matter? Could two different orders both work?
flow.kid: Draw boxes and arrows for your plan. Say why each step is in its place.
flow.parent: A good plan does the dry steps before any water is added. Both a magnet first and a sieve first work, since the pins are not hidden by the chana. The order that fails is adding water first, because then every dry method stops working.

flow.do: Follow your plan. Put each part on its own plate as soon as it is separated. If you need to dissolve the salt, use a little water and stir. Then filter the sand from the salt water. Dry the filtrate on the steel plate in the sun.
flow.say: Is each plate clean? Did any part end up in the wrong place? What would you change?
flow.kid: Follow your plan. Put each part on its own plate.
flow.parent: A usual order is a magnet for the pins and a sieve for the chana. Then water dissolves the salt, a filter catches the sand and evaporation gets the salt. The sand should be rinsed with a little water over the filter so that no salt stays on it. The salt takes a day or two to dry, so look at it later.

flow.do: Look at each plate. Check each one for anything that should not be there. Check the pins with the magnet, and the chana by eye. Look at the sand for white salt specks. Write what you find.
flow.say: Which plate is the cleanest? Where was the plan not quite perfect?
flow.kid: Check each plate for anything out of place. Write what you find.
flow.parent: Sand that was not rinsed leaves a white film of salt when it dries. This is a good test of the plan, and not a mistake in the child.

flow.do: Change one step in your plan. Think about what would be better, such as rinsing the sand once more or sieving with finer holes. Write the change and why you think it would help.
flow.say: If you did it again, what is the one thing you would change? How would you test whether it helped?
flow.kid: Pick one step to change. Say why it would help.
flow.parent: There is no single correct plan. Several can work, and some use fewer steps.
flow.think: Every step uses one difference. What mixture could you make where two parts have no difference you can use?

general: Dry first: pass a magnet through the bowl to take out the pins. Then sieve to take out the chana. Then add water, stir, filter out the sand and dry the salt water on a plate.
Pick the pins and the chana by hand, which is slow but needs no tools. Then use water, a filter and evaporation for the sand and salt.
Use the sieve first, then the magnet. Both orders work, because the pins and the chana are different in different ways.
creative: Dissolve the salt first by pouring water through the whole bowl in a cloth bag. Catch the salt water in a plate below, and the pins, chana and sand stay in the cloth. Then use a magnet and a sieve on the dry cloth contents.
Rinse the sand over the filter with a little extra water, so no salt stays on the sand. Add the rinse water to the plate you dry in the sun.
Pass the magnet through twice, once before the sieve and once after, in case a pin hid under a chana.
challenges.your_turn: Make a new mixture of four things from your kitchen, plan how to separate it, and try it. Which of your steps used a difference you had not thought of at first? Is there a mixture that you could not separate at all?

challenges.title: Clear the muddy water: build a filter and test how clear it gets
challenges.context: This is a design problem. You build a water filter from home things. Then you measure how clear it makes muddy water, using a cross on paper at the bottom of a tumbler.
challenges.problem: Muddy water must be made as clear as you can with a filter you build, using only home things. Measure how clear it gets with a black cross, and improve your filter. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Do not drink the water. Clear water can still carry germs.
Use only things you can find at home, and keep every layer clean.
Test the water with the cross before and after, and use the same amount of muddy water each time.
Change only one thing in the filter between tests.
materials: muddy water made with 2 tablespoons of soil in a litre of water
a clean cotton cloth, a coffee filter paper and cotton wool
washed sand, small clean pebbles and a tea strainer
a clear plastic bottle with the bottom cut off by an adult, and a rubber band
a tall clear tumbler and a sheet of paper with a black cross drawn on it
a clock or phone timer and a pencil

setup.art: A black cross drawn on white paper under a tall clear tumbler, with muddy water being poured in until the cross vanishes.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tumbler slowly until the cross can no longer be seen from above. Measure the depth.

setup.art: A cut plastic bottle held upside down with layers of cloth, sand and pebbles inside, dripping into a tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Build a filter in layers inside a cut bottle.

flow.do: Stir 2 tablespoons of soil into a litre of water. Draw a thick black cross on a white sheet and put a tall clear tumbler on it. Pour muddy water in slowly while you look straight down. Stop when the cross just disappears. Measure the depth of water in the tumbler with a ruler. This is your starting measurement.
flow.say: The cross disappears when the water is deep enough. What do you think will happen to the depth after filtering? Why?
flow.kid: Pour muddy water slowly until the cross disappears. Measure the depth.
flow.parent: Mud makes the water cloudy so that the cross disappears at a few centimetres. A clearer water must be deeper before the cross disappears. This is a simple way to measure how clear water is.

flow.do: An adult cuts the bottom off a clear plastic bottle. Turn it upside down with the neck down. Push a pad of cotton wool into the neck. Rest the bottle in a tall tumbler or hold it above one with a rubber band.
flow.say: A filter works by letting water through and holding the mud back. What do you think should go in first at the bottom, and what at the top?
flow.kid: Ask an adult to cut the bottle. Put cotton wool in the neck. Set it above a tumbler.
flow.parent: An adult should cut the plastic, because the edge can be sharp. Make sure the bottle neck points down into the tumbler.

flow.do: Build your first filter. Put in a layer of cloth, then 3 centimetres of washed sand, then a thin layer of small pebbles. Pour 200 millilitres of muddy water slowly onto the pebbles. Catch the water that comes out. Time how long it takes to drip through.
flow.say: What is happening to the mud as the water goes down? Is the water that comes out clear?
flow.kid: Fill the bottle in layers. Pour muddy water in slowly. Catch what comes out.
flow.parent: The first water that comes through may be cloudy, because the sand still holds dust. Pour the first batch back through, or wash the sand first. A filter may take 5 to 10 minutes.

flow.do: Test the filtered water with the cross, and measure the depth when the cross disappears. Compare with your first measurement. Write both and the difference.
flow.say: How much deeper did the water need to be? Is that clear enough? Is it safe to drink?
flow.kid: Test the filtered water with the cross. Measure the depth. Compare with before.
flow.parent: A deeper measurement means clearer water. Even when the cross shows clearly, the water must not be drunk. The holes in sand and cloth are far bigger than germs. It must be boiled or treated first. Pour the water on plants when you finish.

flow.do: Change one thing in the filter, such as adding a coffee filter paper under the sand or folding the cloth more times. Run the filter again and test with the cross. Write the new depth and say if the change helped.
flow.say: What did you change? Did it help? How do you know that one change did it?
flow.kid: Change one thing in your filter. Test again.
flow.parent: Changing one thing at a time shows which change helped. A sari folded several times was tested in villages in Bangladesh. It cut cholera by about half, so even a plain cloth helps.
flow.think: Clear water looks clean. What would you have to test to be sure it is?

general: Layers of cloth, sand and small pebbles inside a cut bottle, with the coarse layer at the top and the finest at the bottom.
Let the water settle for an hour, pour off the top with care and then filter only the top part.
Use a coffee filter paper in a tea strainer, which has the smallest holes, and pour in a little at a time.
creative: Fold a clean cotton cloth four times and pour water through it, as the village women in Bangladesh were taught.
Use two filters in a row. A coarse one goes first to catch the big bits. A fine one goes second to catch the rest, so it does not clog.
Run the water through a tall narrow tube of sand instead of a wide one, to give the water a longer path.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own filter from things at home and test it with the cross. What did you change that made the water clearer? What would you need to test to know the water is safe?

games.title: The Right Difference: a card game about choosing how to separate
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends.
games.context: This is a card game in which you read a mixture, choose the method that fits, and score points when your choice is right. Some cards have two good answers, so you can defend yours.

setup.art: Eight method cards laid face up in a row, with a pile of mixture cards face down and a small pile of chain cards to one side.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 8 method cards face up in a row. Shuffle the mixture cards into a pile.

setup.art: A player reading a mixture card aloud and placing it below a method card, while another player holds the card's back.
setup.caption: 2. Read a mixture card aloud and place it under the method you choose. Someone checks the back.

printables.title: 8 method cards
items: Picking. Use a difference your eyes or fingers can tell, and take pieces out one at a time.
Sieving. Use a difference in size. Small pieces fall through the holes and big pieces stay on top.
Winnowing. Use moving air. Light pieces are carried away and heavy ones fall straight down.
Settling and pouring off. Use how fast the pieces sink. Heavy pieces sink to the bottom and you tip the clear top away.
Filtering. Use a cloth or paper with holes too small for a solid that has not dissolved. The liquid passes through.
Magnet. Use being attracted. Only iron, steel and a few other metals are pulled out.
Evaporation. Let the water leave as vapour. A dissolved solid cannot follow it, so it stays behind.
Chromatography. Let a liquid creep along wet paper. Each part of a mixture travels at its own speed.

printables.title: 24 mixture cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Steel pins in a bowl of rice. Take out the pins.
items.b: Magnet. Pins are attracted and rice is not. Picking also works, but slowly.

items.f: Husk mixed with paddy grain after harvest. Take out the husk.
items.b: Winnowing. Husk is lighter than grain, so a breeze carries it away.

items.f: Salt dissolved in water. Get the salt back.
items.b: Evaporation. The water leaves as vapour and the salt stays behind.

items.f: Mud mixed in water. Take the mud out.
items.b: Filtering. A cloth or paper holds the mud back. Settling and pouring off also works, but the finest mud stays in the water.

items.f: Small stones in dal. Take the stones out.
items.b: Picking. Stones and dal are close in size, so a sieve does not work well. Tossing the dal in a winnowing tray can also work, since stones are heavier.

items.f: Bran flakes in atta. Take out the bran.
items.b: Sieving. The flour is finer than the holes and the bran flakes are bigger.

items.f: The colours in one black ink. Part the colours.
items.b: Chromatography. Each colour travels up wet paper at its own speed.

items.f: Sand shaken into a jar of water. Take the sand out.
items.b: Settling and pouring off. Sand sinks quickly. Filtering also works.

items.f: Iron filings in sugar. Take out the iron.
items.b: Magnet. Iron is attracted and sugar is not. Do not dissolve the sugar first, because the dry methods come first.

items.f: Tea leaves in tea. Take out the leaves.
items.b: Filtering. A strainer holds the leaves back and lets the tea pass.

items.f: Chana in a bowl of rice. Take out the chana.
items.b: Sieving. Rice falls through a colander and chana stays on top. Picking also works.

items.f: Sea water in a salt pan. Get the salt.
items.b: Evaporation. The Sun takes the water and the salt is left.

items.f: Dust blown into wheat on a threshing floor. Take out the dust.
items.b: Winnowing. Dust is light and moves away on the wind.

items.f: Pebbles mixed into building sand. Take out the pebbles.
items.b: Sieving. Sand falls through the holes and the pebbles stay.

items.f: Soil washed into rain water in a bucket. Clear the water.
items.b: Settling and pouring off, or filtering. Soil sinks, and a cloth then holds back the rest.

items.f: Pulp in orange juice. Make the juice clear.
items.b: Filtering. A strainer or cloth holds the pulp back.

items.f: Needles dropped into a box of cotton. Take them out.
items.b: Magnet. Steel needles are attracted and cotton is not.

items.f: Sugar dissolved in water. Get the sugar back.
items.b: Evaporation. Let the water leave slowly and the sugar is left.

items.f: The colours in a green food dye. Part them.
items.b: Chromatography. A green dye is often a mix of blue and yellow, and they climb at different speeds.

items.f: Rotten beans among good beans. Take out the rotten ones.
items.b: Picking. They differ in colour and softness, which eyes and fingers can tell.

items.f: Straw bits in grain on a windy day. Take out the straw.
items.b: Winnowing. Straw is light and the wind blows it away from the heavy grain.

items.f: Curd lumps in whey. Take out the lumps.
items.b: Filtering. A muslin cloth holds the lumps back and lets the whey through.

items.f: Mud in a pond after rain. Make the water clear without a filter.
items.b: Settling and pouring off. Leave the water still and the mud sinks in time.

items.f: Rajma and iron nails in a jar. Take out the nails.
items.b: Magnet. Iron nails are attracted and rajma is not.

printables.title: 6 chain cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Chain card. Iron pins, sand and salt, all dry. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Magnet first, to take out the pins while everything is dry. Then stir the rest into water and filter, which holds the sand back. Then evaporate the filtrate to get the salt.

items.f: Chain card. Rice, husk and small stones. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Winnow first to blow the husk away. Then pick out the stones, or sieve them if they are bigger than the grains. Then wash the rice and pour off the dust.

items.f: Chain card. Mud, salt and water. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Let the mud settle and pour off the top. Filter the top water through paper until it is clear. Then evaporate the clear water to get the salt.

items.f: Chain card. Iron nails, sugar and gravel. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Magnet first, to take out the nails. Then stir the rest into water so the sugar dissolves, and pick or sieve out the gravel. Then evaporate the sugar water.

items.f: Chain card. Steel pins, chana and atta. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Both orders work. Use a magnet for the pins, and a flour sieve for the atta, which falls through while chana stays. The order does not matter here, so a player who defends either order scores.

items.f: Chain card. Pebbles, sand and salty water. Give the steps in order.
items.b: Pour through a sieve to hold back the pebbles. Filter the rest through cloth to hold back the sand. Then evaporate the filtrate to get the salt.

rules: Lay the 8 method cards face up in a row. Shuffle the 24 mixture cards. Deal 4 to each player and put the rest face down as a draw pile. Keep the 6 chain cards in a separate pile, face down.

On your turn, choose one mixture card from your hand. Read the front aloud. Place it under the method card you think fits, and say in one sentence why that method uses a difference the parts really have.

The player on your left turns the card over and reads the back. If your method is on the back, keep the card and score 2 points. If the back gives a different method, put the card in the discard pile and the player who read it scores 1.
Some cards have two good answers. If your method is not on the back but you can defend it in one sentence, the table votes. If most players agree it works, you keep the card and score 2 points.

Instead of a mixture card, you may once in the game draw a chain card, read the front aloud and give three steps in order. Then turn it over. Score 1 point for each step that is right and in the right place, up to 3 points.
After each turn, draw a card to have 4 again, if there are cards left. When the draw pile is empty, play on until every hand is empty.
A player whose hand is empty still reads the backs of cards for the others.
The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, deal yourself 10 mixture cards, place each one, check the back and count your points out of 20. Try to beat your own best score.
Say one new fact each time you read a back, so the table learns something from each card.

flow.do: Cut out the 38 cards from the printed sheets. Cut along the lines and keep the front and back of each card together. Shuffle the 24 mixture cards. Lay the 8 method cards in a row, face up. Read the method cards together.
flow.say: Each method uses one difference. Here are eight methods. Let us read what each one uses before we play.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay the method cards in a row. Read each one.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. If you do not print, copy each card on a small piece of paper and write the answer on the back. Keep the cards in an envelope afterwards.

flow.do: Play one practice round together with the cards face up. Pick a mixture card, choose a method and check the back, and talk about why it is or is not right.
flow.say: Let us try one together. What is the difference between the parts? Which method uses it?
flow.kid: Play one round with the cards face up. Pick a card and choose a method together.
flow.parent: Ask 'What is different about the part that leaves?' for each card. That question is the whole game.

flow.do: Play the game with all the rules. Take turns. When a card has two answers, let the table vote. Count the points at the end.
flow.say: Which method will you pick for this one? Why? Can someone argue for a different method?
flow.kid: Play the game. Place each card under a method. Check the back.

ask.q: Which card could be done two ways, and why?
good: Pins in rice can be done with a magnet or by picking.
Chana in rice can be done with a sieve or by picking.

flow.parent: Some cards are meant to have two answers, such as chana in rice or pins in rice. Let the child argue. A game is a game first, and arguing about answers is part of it.

flow.do: Count the points and say who won. Talk about one card where two methods worked. Ask the child to say which they prefer and why.
flow.say: Which was the hardest card? Did any card have two methods that worked? How would you decide between them?
flow.kid: Count the points. Pick a card where two methods worked and say which you prefer.
flow.parent: A good method is one that uses a difference that is easy to use, quick and does not harm the other parts. Neither answer is wrong when both work.
flow.think: Every card needed a difference between the parts. What would you do with a mixture that has no difference at all?

worksheets.title: Mixtures and the difference that separates them (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks what a mixture is and asks you to pick a method that uses the difference between the parts.

items.p: Which one is a mixture of two materials?
opts: A cup of rice with a few small stones
items.why: Rice and stones are two materials, each still itself. A single stone or a cup of one grain is one material. If you picked another, you looked for two different materials together.

items.p: Salt stirred into water has stopped being salt, because you cannot see it.
items.why: False. The water tastes salty and evaporation brings the salt back. The pieces are too small to see, but they are still salt.

items.p: Iron pins mixed into sand are still attracted by a ____.
items.why: Iron keeps its own property of being attracted, even when it is mixed with sand. The sand does not change it.

items.p: A sieve separates the parts of a mixture by a difference in what?
items.why: A sieve lets pieces smaller than its holes through and holds back bigger ones. Colour and taste play no part, so if you picked them you were thinking of picking by eye or tongue.

items.p: Sort each mixture by the method that fits best.
items: steel pins in rice
Magnet
stones bigger than rice grains, in rice
Sieve
salt dissolved in water, when you want the salt
Evaporation
soil mud floating in water
Filter
bran flakes in atta
Sieve
items.why: Each method uses one difference. A magnet uses being attracted, a sieve uses size, evaporation leaves a dissolved solid behind and a filter holds back a solid that has not dissolved.

items.p: Match each tool to the difference it uses.
pairs: a winnowing tray in the breeze
a solid that has not dissolved
items.why: A tool works because the parts of the mixture differ in the one way it uses. Each tool treats the parts differently for just one reason.

items.p: Put these steps in order to get salt out of muddy salt water.
a: Stir the mud and salt into water
Pour the muddy water through filter paper
Leave the clear water on a plate in the sun
Look at the white crust left on the plate
items.why: The filter takes out the mud first, because the mud would spoil the crust. Evaporation comes last, because the water must leave for the dissolved salt to be left.

items.p: You pour tea through a strainer. What stays behind in the strainer?
items.why: The solid that stays behind is the residue. The tea that passes through is the filtrate. If you chose the filtrate, you named the wrong part.

items.p: Rice and dal are mixed in a cup. Explain why this is a mixture and not a new material.
items.a: Each stays itself. A grain of rice is still rice and a grain of dal is still dal. You can pick them apart again and get the same rice and the same dal. Nothing new was made.
items.why: A strong answer says that each material keeps its properties and can be taken out again unchanged.

items.p: Iron pins, sand and salt are all dry. What is the best first step?
opts: Heat all of it on a stove
items.why: A magnet works only on dry pieces, and takes out the pins cleanly. Adding water first would make the pins wet and the sand and salt harder to handle. Heating would not separate anything.

items.p: Evaporation takes the salt out of salt water and leaves the water behind.
items.why: False. Evaporation takes the water away as vapour and leaves the dissolved salt behind.

items.p: Draw boxes and arrows showing how to separate steel pins, rice and salt. Write the method in each box.
items.a: Four boxes in order. A magnet takes the pins out of the dry mix. Water and stirring dissolve the salt. A cloth holds the rice back. Evaporation leaves the salt.
items.why: A good plan does the dry method first and uses a different difference for each step.

items.p: Your lungs take oxygen from the air you breathe in. What is that job?
items.why: Air is a mixture of gases. Lungs take some oxygen out and leave the rest. Lungs do not make oxygen and do not mix the air.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Milk with lemon, salt in water, sand in water, pins in rice.
items.a: Milk with lemon, because a new material is made and the milk cannot come back. The other three are mixtures whose parts can be taken out again.
items.why: A mixture keeps its parts. When materials join to form a new material, a chemical change has happened.

items.p: Is a glass of clear tap water pure?

views.who: Indian food safety rules and shop labels
views.says: Pure means clean and safe, with nothing added that should not be there.
Pure means one substance only, and tap water holds dissolved minerals and gases.

items.ask: Which meaning of pure would you use for your drinking water, and why?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that both are useful for different jobs. Safe is what matters for drinking, and one substance only is what matters in a chemistry test.
items.why: Both meanings are true in their own place. Words like pure depend on which test or purpose is in mind.

items.p: A friend says 'clear water is just water'. What could you do to find out if it holds anything else?
items.a: Dry a spoonful on a clean plate and look for a ring or crust left. Compare with a second plate of water that is known to be clean. Taste is not safe for every water.
items.why: A strong answer uses a test that can find a dissolved solid, such as evaporation, since the eye cannot see it.

worksheets.title: Choosing, testing and explaining (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to plan several steps, compare different views and apply separating to living beings and the Earth.

items.p: A sieve has 3 millimetre holes. Which one is stopped by it?
items.why: Only pieces bigger than the holes stay on top. The bean is bigger than 3 millimetres and the grain and dust are smaller.

items.p: Which of these can a magnet NOT separate from sand?
items.why: A magnet attracts iron and steel and does not attract salt, so it cannot take salt out of sand. If you picked a metal, remember that metals like iron are attracted.

items.p: If filtered water looks clear, it is safe to drink.
items.why: False. The holes in cloth and paper are bigger than germs, and dissolved things pass straight through. Clear only means that no solid pieces big enough to see are left.

items.p: Lemon juice is stirred into hot milk and the milk curdles. Why is this not a separation?
items.why: Curdling is a chemical change, so the parts cannot be taken out as they were. If you picked dissolving, remember that dissolved things can be recovered by evaporation.

items.p: Sort each separation by the difference it uses.
items: atta sieve holding back bran
Size
scrap dealer lifting iron with a big magnet
Attracted by a magnet
adding water so salt dissolves and sand does not
Dissolving
rice sinking while dust stays cloudy in the wash water
How fast it sinks
items.why: Each tool or step uses one difference. Naming the difference tells you whether it can work on a new mixture.

items.p: Put these in order of hole size, smallest first.
items.why: Filter paper holes are about one hundredth of a millimetre. Cloth threads leave gaps of about a tenth of a millimetre. An atta sieve has holes under 1 millimetre and a colander has holes of a few millimetres.

items.p: Match each one to the separating it does.
pairs: Takes small animals and algae from muddy water
Stops most salt from sea water
Leaves salt behind in the sea
items.why: Living beings and the Earth use the same kinds of differences that people use, such as size and which materials pass through.

items.p: A mixture holds iron nails, sugar and sand. Plan the steps and say what difference each one uses.
items.a: Magnet first, which uses being attracted, to take out the nails. Then add water, which uses dissolving, so the sugar dissolves and the sand does not. Then filter, which holds back the sand. Then evaporate the water to get the sugar.
items.why: A good plan does dry methods first and names one difference for each step.

items.p: Why wait before pouring off the clear water from muddy water?
opts: Mud sinks in time and the top clears
items.why: Heavier pieces sink if you wait, so the top becomes clearer. Mud does not dissolve or become water, so do not expect it to vanish.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the sea and a cloud. Show where the salt stays when rain forms.
items.a: The Sun shines on the sea. Arrows rise from the sea to the cloud for water vapour. Salt is shown staying in the sea, with none in the cloud.
items.why: Evaporation lifts water but not salt, so rain from sea water is fresh.

items.p: Should household waste be mixed and sorted later, or kept apart at home?

views.says: Keep it apart at home. Wet food waste ruins paper and plastic I can sell, and sorting mixed waste is dirty and takes hours.

views.who: A busy city official (an imagined view)
views.says: Many households will not sort. It may be better to collect everything and sort it at a plant with machines and paid workers.

items.ask: Whose job is the sorting in each view, and who benefits?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says who does the work and who is paid in each view, and notes that a plant needs workers too.
items.why: Both views have trade-offs. Mixing is easy for the person who throws, and separating always costs work for someone.

items.p: Air is one material, because we cannot see its parts.
items.why: False. Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Parts too small to see can still be there.

items.p: A test finds nothing else in a water sample. What can the scientist say?
opts: It passed the test she used
items.why: A test only finds what it can catch. A new test may still find more, so 'pure' tells you which tests the sample has passed.

items.p: Winnowing works because moving air carries ____ pieces farther than heavy ones.
items.why: Husk is light and grain is heavy, so a breeze blows the husk farther while the grain falls in a heap.

items.p: Sugar stirred into tea looks gone. Which of its properties stayed, and which seem lost?
items.a: The sweet taste stayed. The white colour, the crunch and the shape seem lost, because the pieces are too small to see. The sugar is still there and can be got back by evaporation.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sugar keeps its properties, even if some are hidden at the scale of the eye.

items.p: A river slows down. Which pieces does it drop first?
items.why: Heavy pieces sink first as the water slows. Fine clay sinks last and dissolved salt does not sink at all.

worksheets.title: Faulty sums and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks about harder mixtures, hidden parts, how pure is pure and the questions that are still open.

items.p: Sand and sugar are left. Water is added and stirred. What next?
opts: Filter, to hold back the sand
Sieve, to hold back the sugar
items.why: Sugar dissolves and passes through the filter with the water. Sand stays on the filter. The sugar is too small to sieve or pick.

items.p: If two tests cannot tell two samples apart, they are certainly the same material.
items.why: False. A new test may find a difference. Heavy hydrogen was found in 1931, and after that a jar of water could be described as a mixture.

items.p: The Sun heats the sea and a cloud forms. Why is rain not salty?
opts: Salt cannot leave with the vapour
items.why: Evaporation takes only the water. Salt is left behind in the sea. Salt is not destroyed and clouds are not filters.

items.p: A sand grain 0.5 millimetres wide meets paper holes 0.01 millimetres wide. The grain is ____ times wider.
items.why: 0.5 ÷ 0.01 = 50. The grain cannot get through the hole, so the paper holds sand back easily.

items.p: Two tumblers of the same plain water are poured together. Did mixing happen? Give one reason for yes and one for no.
items.a: Yes: the molecules from the two tumblers spread among each other. No: no test can find any change, because the two are exactly alike. Scientists still argue about whether mixing is a fact about the materials or about what our tests can tell apart.
items.why: A strong answer gives both views and notes that the question is still open.

items.p: Brass is made of copper and zinc. What can be true of brass?
opts: It has no properties of its own
items.why: A mixture of metals can have properties that neither part has alone. Brass is harder than copper. This is why people make alloys.

items.p: Put these in order to clean rice with stones, husk and fine dust.
a: Wash the rice and pour off the dusty water
items.why: Do the dry methods first. Wet methods come last, because water would mix the dust and starch into the rice.

items.p: A 22-carat gold bangle is a mixture.
items.why: True. Of every 24 parts, 22 are gold and 2 are other metals, such as copper or silver. It looks like one metal, but it is an alloy.

items.p: Argon was found when nitrogen from air weighed a bit more than nitrogen made in a lab. What does this show?
opts: A small difference can reveal a hidden part
items.why: The air sample held a heavier gas mixed in, which turned out to be argon. A careful test finds what an earlier one missed.

items.p: Is mixing a fact about materials, or about what our tests can tell apart?

views.says: Mixing depends on which differences we can keep track of. A new way to tell things apart turns one material into a mixture.

views.who: Many physicists who work with quantum physics
views.says: Two particles of the same kind are exactly alike, so whether two samples are different is a plain fact and not a matter of our tests.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing, and what would you want to test?
items.a: Answers vary, and scientists still disagree. A strong answer gives a reason from the two tumbler example.
items.why: Neither view is marked right, because the question is still debated.

items.p: Name one way a living being separates a mixture, and say what difference it uses.
items.a: A kidney filters blood and keeps the useful materials while letting waste go, using the size and kind of each material. A flamingo's beak strains small animals out of muddy water, using size.
items.why: A strong answer names the being, the mixture and the difference.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Sieving, winnowing, evaporating, picking.
items.a: Evaporating, because it separates something dissolved from its liquid. The other three sort solid pieces that you can still see.
items.why: A dissolved solid is in pieces too small to see, so sieving and picking cannot reach it.

items.p: A magnet can lift every metal out of a mixture.
items.why: False. A magnet attracts iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Aluminium, copper and gold are not pulled.

items.p: A kidney filters about 180 litres a day but passes about 1.5 litres. Where does the rest go?
items.why: Nearly all of the filtered liquid is taken back into the blood. Only the waste and a little water leave as urine.

items.p: Draw a filter for muddy water. Label the layers and show where the mud is held.
items.a: A cut bottle upside down, with cotton wool at the neck, a layer of sand and a layer of pebbles at the top. Arrows show the water passing through, with mud caught in the sand and a label that clear water may still carry germs.
items.why: A good drawing shows the coarse layer first and the fine layer after, and notes that the water is not yet safe.

items.p: Sieving cannot separate sugar from sand, but adding water can. Explain why.
items.a: Sugar and sand grains are about the same size, so a sieve cannot tell them apart. Sugar dissolves in water and sand does not, so water uses a difference that a sieve does not.
items.why: A strong answer names the difference that works (dissolving) and the one that does not (size).

quiz.p: Sugar is stirred into tea and seems to vanish. What is the best description?
opts: Still there, in pieces too small to see
quiz.why: The tea tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there. If you chose the other answers, you may have thought that unseen means gone.

quiz.p: Which test best shows that lemon in milk made a new material?
opts: You cannot get the smooth milk back
quiz.why: A mixture can be taken apart and give back each part unchanged. Colour and taste do not tell you that.

quiz.p: A magnet lifts steel pins out of sand. Why did the sand not change the pins?
opts: Materials keep their properties in a mixture
quiz.why: The pins are still attracted, because mixing does not change what a material is. Sand is not magnetic, and weight is not what the magnet uses.

quiz.p: Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water. What does this show?
opts: A mixture can have a property its parts lack alone
quiz.why: The whole mixture can have a new property, even though each part keeps its own. Freezing point is one of them.

quiz.p: Which difference is easiest to use to separate chalk powder from iron filings?
quiz.why: Iron is attracted by a magnet and chalk is not. The magnet leaves the chalk behind. Colour and taste are poor tools here.

quiz.p: A filter clears muddy water, but the water is still salty. Why?
opts: Dissolved salt is too small to be held back
quiz.why: Dissolved salt is in pieces far smaller than the filter's holes, so it passes through with the water.

quiz.p: You dry a spoon of salt water on a plate. Why also dry a spoon of plain tap water?
opts: To see what the tap water alone leaves
To make the salt water dry faster
quiz.why: The tap water may leave a faint ring, and the second plate shows how much. Then you do not give the salt credit for it.

quiz.p: Which order works for gravel, sugar and iron nails?
opts: Magnet, then water and filter, then evaporate
quiz.why: The dry magnet comes first. Then water dissolves the sugar, so gravel is caught by the filter, and evaporation gives the sugar back.

quiz.p: Why does mixed rubbish cost a waste picker more work than rubbish kept apart?
opts: Mixing is easy but separating always needs work
quiz.why: Mixing happens by itself, but taking things apart needs effort from a hand, a machine or the Sun.

quiz.p: Sweat dries on a shirt and leaves a white mark. What does this show?
opts: Salt stayed when the water evaporated
quiz.why: The water left as vapour and the salt could not follow, the same as in a salt pan.

quiz.p: Bees make honey from nectar that is more than half water. Which separation is that?
quiz.why: The water leaves the nectar, and the sugars stay behind, so the honey is thick.

quiz.p: A bottle says '99.9 per cent pure'. Why does it not say 100?
opts: No test can show that nothing else is there
quiz.why: A test only shows what it can find. A finer test may find more, so purity is given as a number.

quiz.p: Which question about mixing has no agreed answer yet?
opts: Why the universe began in such an orderly state
quiz.why: Physicists can explain why mixing is likely, but not yet why the universe began so orderly.

quiz.p: Black ink splits into blue, pink and yellow on wet paper. What made the colours spread apart?
opts: They climb the paper at different speeds
quiz.why: Each colour is carried along by the water and clings to the paper by a different amount, so it travels at its own speed.
